# CAD modeling and inspection

A model is a Python function; running its script rebuilds it in text-to-cad's warm server, and
the page the person has open updates. Files are exports, made when asked.

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Create or edit a part or assembly** | The project's model script, or a new one ([below](#write-a-model-and-run-it)); a part the request says how to make is designed for that process from the first line ([Design for the process](#design-for-the-process)). | [Models](references/model-contract.md), [build123d](references/build123d-modeling.md), [positioning](references/positioning.md) |
| **Organize a CAD project** | The project's existing layout. | [Project layout](references/project-layout.md) |
| **Export STEP, STL, 3MF, GLB or xbf** | `cad model export <id> <file>`. | [Exports](references/exports.md) |
| **Make a 2D profile, flat pattern or DXF** | A model that returns 2D geometry on z=0, then `cad model export <id> part.dxf`. | [2D profiles and DXF](references/2d-profiles-and-dxf.md) |
| **Use a vendor STEP, an xbf or a scan in a model** | `step.read`, `xbf.read` or `stl.read` in the body. | [Inputs](references/model-contract.md#inputs) |

## Setup and paths

Run the `cad` command (`~/.local/bin/cad` where it is not on your PATH; `cad.exe` on Windows). If
it is missing, install text-to-cad, outside a sandbox or with its permission:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://texttocad.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://www.texttocad.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. If the CAD app was
only just added, its server may still be starting: try again for up to a minute first. `cad doctor
--check` explains any other failure, changing nothing; `cad doctor` repairs what it reports. Tell the
person any next step `cad setup` prints.

One server runs for the installation: the first run starts it, every run and every
command goes through it, and it serves the viewer. `cad status` lists its workers
and the documents it holds; `cad stop` stops it.
A build cut off by the shell's time limit keeps running in the server; run the same
command again and it waits for that build and replays it (`cad status` shows it).
Give a cold build of a large model the shell tool's longest timeout, or run it in the
background.

Build every model with `cad run`, exactly like `uv run`: the same options and the same script
header, with nothing to set up. cad is pinned to this computer's release and its integrations come
from the script's imports (`import build123d` is the build123d integration), so a header names only
the script's own packages, never a version of cad:

```python
# /// script
# dependencies = ["pandas>=2"]
# ///
```

A one-off dependency is `--with`; a script inside a Python project runs with the project's
dependencies and lock. A run that stops on an import or a requirement says what to change in one
line. [Environments](references/environments.md) has the details: `--with`, projects and their locks,
private indexes and the network.

Command-line paths, and the paths `step.read`, `xbf.read`, `stl.read` and a type's `export`
take, are relative to the working directory, as are a model's own file reads. Anchor
them on `__file__` in code that must run from any folder.

## Write a model and run it

A part or an assembly is a function with no parameters, decorated `@model` (or with its
file decorators, never both), that returns a build123d shape. Its dimensions are the
arguments of a plain helper function, and each configuration is a `@model` of its own, with
its own id and page; constants several models share live in a module they import. A call
builds it and returns its document: a handle with `.id`, `.url`, `.shape` (the built shape)
and `.export(...)`. For example, `src/bracket.py`:

```python
import build123d as bd
from cad import model


def bracket_body(width, thickness, bore):
    body = bd.Box(width, 20, thickness)
    hole = bd.Cylinder(bore / 2, thickness)
    body = body - hole
    body.label = "bracket"
    body.color = "#4a6fa5"
    return body


@model
def bracket():
    return bracket_body(40, 6, 8)


@model
def bracket_wide():
    return bracket_body(60, 6, 8)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    bracket()
    bracket_wide()
```

```bash
cad run src/bracket.py
```

```text
built src/bracket.py::bracket cold in 2.61s: bodies 1 run; 6 misses, 0 hits; body 0.01s, names 0.00s, document 0.00s
  parts 1 · bounds 40 × 20 × 6 mm · joints 0 · sequences 0
  id: 0dc50a92-a21f-5895-a245-ebdeb5352f3b
  view: http://127.0.0.1:54360/0dc50a92-a21f-5895-a245-ebdeb5352f3b?token=...
built src/bracket.py::bracket_wide warm in 0.01s: bodies 1 run; 6 misses, 0 hits; body 0.01s, names 0.00s, document 0.00s
  parts 1 · bounds 60 × 20 × 6 mm · joints 0 · sequences 0
  id: 966d03a5-7b43-5bed-b75c-eb67d56c72d2
  view: http://127.0.0.1:54360/966d03a5-7b43-5bed-b75c-eb67d56c72d2?token=...
```

Each call the script's `__main__` makes prints how its model built, the delta under it
(parts, bounds, joints and sequences), its document's `id:` and its page, `view:` (the
handle's `.id` and `.url`). An unchanged rerun prints `took ... nothing ran` instead. Give the
user the page once ([Show the model](#show-the-model)) and use the id for every command
after it. The id comes from the
script's path and the function's name, or the script's folder and an explicit `@model(name="...")`,
so it is the same run after run, and the open page follows every run. A model's name is its identity
within its namespace, the function's name by default, `name=` gives it another. The namespace
is the script's folder; two explicit names in it must differ.

- **Running the script is the rebuild.** It writes no file. The server's warm worker for
  the script replays every operation an edit did not reach, so a comment re-runs nothing
  and a dimension edit re-runs what reads it
  ([what a run runs](references/model-contract.md#what-a-run-runs)). Decoration only
  declares: keep the calls under `if __name__ == "__main__":` so other scripts can import
  the models.
- **`@memo` marks stages, never parts.** The server already replays every kernel call, so
  mark only a function holding seconds of kernel work that an edit elsewhere leaves
  alone, such as a whole sub-assembly stage; never a part, never a helper called many
  times ([`@memo`](references/model-contract.md#memo-marks-stages)).
- **An assembly calls its parts.** Its body calls each part model and composes its shape
  (`plate().shape`), places and labels it, and returns a `Compound`. Each child builds in
  the same run and keeps its own document and id. Running a child's script alone leaves the assemblies that
  use it as they were: run the assembly.
- **`import build123d as bd`, and use it attribute-style** (`bd.Box`). The import is lazy:
  the kernel loads on first use, in the worker. `from build123d import Box`, or a
  module-level `bd.Color(...)` or `bd.Align` default, loads it at that line instead.
- **Colours are sRGB**, as a person picks them: `part.color = "#4a6fa5"` (`"#4a6fa5cc"` with
  alpha). `part.color` is build123d's: it takes no 0-255 integers (OCCT's `Color out`), which
  `paint` does. Import `metals` from `bd_materials`; assign a native material with
  `part.material = metals.aluminum()` (the families and their materials are listed in
  [colour and materials](references/build123d-modeling.md#colour-and-materials); plain steel is
  `metals.mild_steel()`); boards, electronic parts and finishes (solder mask, ENIG, anodized,
  powder coat) are `cad.build123d.materials`' named looks.
- **Inputs** are `step.read`, `xbf.read` and `stl.read` in the body, and any file its
  Python opens, each tracked by its bytes. The clock, environment variables and
  randomness are not seen: a body is a function of its code and its inputs. Compose
  project models by calling them, never by reading a file the project exported.
- **References** to faces, edges and parts come from `cad model inspect <id> [ref]`, and the
  body picks the same element with build123d's selectors; verify with a snapshot when in
  doubt ([references](references/inspection-and-validation.md#references)).
- **A shape with no function** (a notebook cell, a REPL) is handed over:
  `model(shape, name="plate")` returns the same handle, and no command builds it again.
- **The server never reruns code.** A restart reopens every document from the server's
  cache, as last built. When the cache holds no file of one (deleted by hand, or never
  saved), the page, `cad model inspect <id>` and `cad_show` print the command that brings it
  back (`cad run src/bracket.py`). Run it.
- Model units are millimetres, +Z up.
- An image without a scale sets no fit dimension, and a drawing's units, projection and
  revision decide how its numbers read. A missing or conflicting dimension that changes
  the result is the person's to settle; a value chosen in its place is an assumption.

## Files, when asked

A file is an action on the document the server holds, never part of the model: no code
change and no rebuild, written at once. It holds what the document held when it was
written, so a change made after it is in the file only once it is written again. Write one
when the person asks for it:

```bash
cad model export "$ID" STEP/bracket.step STL/bracket.stl GLB/bracket.glb 3MF/bracket.3mf
```

A project with standing deliverables gets an `exports.py` that imports its models and
calls `model.export(x, path, ...)` on each (`from cad import model`; `x` a model call's handle); running it rewrites every deliverable
([exports](references/exports.md)). An export takes a document and its destinations,
and nothing else: a posed file is a model that returns the posed assembly
(`posed(arm(), "folded")`), and a part on its own is the part's own model. A DXF is the export of a
model that returns 2D geometry, a profile or a flat pattern, and a solid is refused
([2D profiles and DXF](references/2d-profiles-and-dxf.md)). An STL or 3MF for printing a part with fits takes
`--tolerance MM`, about a tenth of its smallest clearance ([print tolerance](references/exports.md#print-tolerance)); a
GLB for another renderer takes `--tolerance MM --angle DEG` ([a GLB for another renderer](references/exports.md#a-glb-for-another-renderer)).
Those options mesh a GLB, an STL or a 3MF and nothing else, so an export that takes them names
only those files: a STEP, an xbf or a DXF among them refuses the whole export, nothing written.
Write the other files in an export of their own:

```bash
cad model export "$ID" STEP/bracket.step GLB/bracket.glb
cad model export "$ID" STL/bracket.stl 3MF/bracket.3mf --tolerance 0.02
```

The xbf, text-to-cad's own document, is Save As: export one only to share a model without its
code, or to compose it in another project with `xbf.read`. A restart needs none: the
server's own cache reopens every document it built, as last built. A vendor STEP is
converted to an xbf once
(`cad step export vendor/motor.step vendor/motor.xbf`) and read with `xbf.read`, many
times faster than parsing the STEP.

## Projects built around exported files

A project can instead revolve around its exported files, but only when the person asks to
iterate on the exported file itself or the project already does: an `exports.py`, a consumer
that reads the files (a robot description, a slicer, a drawing pipeline), or a 0.7-era
layout, whose runs wrote files. The loop is three steps. The script writes the file on each
run, by a file decorator in place of `@model` (`@step("../STEP/bracket.step")`, relative to
the script), or `exports.py` or `cad <type> export` follows the run. Show the file's page, not
the model's: it follows the file on disk, updating when a run rewrites the file.
Verification reads the file: `cad <type> snapshot` or `cad <type> inspect` with its path, or
`step.read` in a check. The costs keep the default the default: each iteration pays the
file's translation and the page's re-read, a STEP parsed again; a file names no model, so a
ref picked on its page has no `made_by` and a Quick Edit from it no way back into the code;
and the model's page stays the better place to look while editing.
[Exports](references/exports.md#model-page-or-file-page) tables the triggers and costs.

## Prompt references and inspection

A reference such as `0dc50a92-a21f-5895-a245-ebdeb5352f3b#bracket/face 7` names geometry
in a document by the server's own names: the document (a model's id, or a file's
absolute path), `#`, a part or an assembly by the labels on its way from the root
(`hand/finger.2` is the second component labelled `finger` in `hand`), then, after a
slash, one element by its name (`f:`, `e:`, `v:`) or its number (`face 7`). The CAD
viewer copies them. When a prompt names one, resolve it with `cad <type> inspect`:

```bash
cad model inspect "$ID" "bracket/face 7"
```

It answers in JSON what the ref names, placed where its occurrence stands: an element's
canonical `ref`, `kind`, `ordinal` and `name`, the kernel's facts (a face's `area`,
`centroid`, `surface`, `box`, `radius`; an edge's length and endpoints) and `made_by`,
the function, file and line of the code that made it; a part's or an assembly's volume
and mass. Edit the code `made_by` names, or pick the element in the body with
build123d's selectors (`body.faces().sort_by(bd.Axis.Z)[-1]`) matching those facts. A
ref resolves in the document as the latest run left it; one that names nothing, or
several things where it names one, is refused with what it could mean. The grammar is
in [references](references/inspection-and-validation.md#references).

A Quick Edit prompt names its document under `File:` (a model's id, or a file's path:
relative to your workspace, else from `~/`), selected entities under `References:`, and a
snapshot packet as inline JSON or a `.snapshot.json` path. Save inline JSON to a temporary `.snapshot.json`, and draw the view the person
drew their ink in, ink included:

```bash
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/quick_edit.png --annotation tmp/bracket.snapshot.json --camera authored
```

Inspect supplied annotations before editing. Without annotations, the captured view is
optional context; render it when useful to the request. After editing, run the script and
draw it again to check the change
([annotations and Quick Edit views](references/snapshot-review.md#annotations-and-quick-edit-views)).

A reference into a file that is not a document names what the viewer picked in it, in
that file's own terms (none is a ref `cad <type> inspect` resolves):

| File | Reference | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| URDF, SRDF | `/work/arm/arm.urdf#upper_arm` | the link `upper_arm` |
| GLB | `/work/out/model.glb#n12` | the glTF node `nodes[12]` (0-based, the file's own index) |
| 3MF | `/work/out/plate.3mf#o2.1` | the 2nd `<build><item>`'s 1st `<component>` (1-based); `#o3` is the 3rd build item |
| STL | the file alone, on `File:` | one mesh: nothing in it is picked |
| DXF | `/work/DXF/panel.dxf#h2F` | the modelspace entity whose handle is `2F`; what a block reference draws is named by its INSERT |

## Check each change

After every run, read its line and the delta under it (parts, bounds, joints, sequences): a
contradiction with what you intended is fixed before anything else. Then check the change the way it
can be checked:

| The change | Check it with |
| --- | --- |
| A number the person gave: a bound, a distance, a volume | An assert inside the model's body on what the geometry measures, or `cad model inspect`; never by restating the constant, never by code after the call in the script |
| A number the design implies: a clearance, a fit, a mass | A check script that calls the model ([below](#check-scripts)) |
| An assembly: parts added, moved or resized, a joint's travel | `cad model interference "$ID"`, with a `--pose` for each mechanism state and for each sequence at the times that matter ([below](#check-scripts)): no two parts share volume, exactly; a pair it could not measure is not a pass |
| New parts, placements, colours, a mechanism | The snapshots it takes to judge it: usually one from the angle that shows the change, more only when a view leaves the question open, a posed one for a mechanism state |
| A reference the prompt names | `cad model inspect "$ID" '<ref>'` ([Prompt references](#prompt-references-and-inspection)) |
| A 2D profile or DXF | `cad model export` (it runs the drawing checks), then an `ezdxf` read and `cad dxf snapshot` of the file ([check a drawing](references/2d-profiles-and-dxf.md#check-a-drawing)) |
| Any change to the geometry of a part whose process the request names or implies | Its process's check, with the same flags as before: the script's `Check:` line (`cad model dfm "$ID" ...`, [Design for the process](#design-for-the-process)); an error is fixed before anything else, a new warning fixed or reported |

```bash
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/review.png
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/top.png --camera top --display hidden-line
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/open.png --pose open
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/mid.png --pose cycle@2.5   # a configuration sequence, at a time of it
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/lit.png --preview          # lit in a studio: the picture for a person
```

A snapshot draws the document as the viewer does, rendered by OCCT, and writes nothing but the PNG.
Its options say how the picture is drawn: camera (`--camera top`), display, grid, pose and size
([snapshots](references/snapshot-review.md)). For a large assembly, isolate the parts the edit
touched or hide what covers them, instead of drawing the whole model.

- A number is never read off a picture: a snapshot shows arrangement and appearance, not dimensions.
- In an assembly, look at a part alone before it is placed, then the parts that move together, then a
  joint at both ends of its travel, and only then the whole, from behind as well as the front: a cover
  that half encloses what it covers is a few pixels of the whole model's picture and most of its own.
- A check that fails or cannot decide has shown nothing about the design.
- A retry that leaves out or shrinks a specified feature (a fillet skipped, a radius reduced) builds a
  different design from the one asked for.

### Joint stops

`cad <type> ranges` (`model`, `xbf`, `step`) finds each joint's stops from the parts themselves:
it turns or slides each joint alone from the as-built pose, the others as built, a degree or a
millimetre at a time each way, until the parts meet.

```bash
cad model ranges "$ID"
cad model ranges "$ID" --joint gripper
cad step ranges arm.step --step 0.5 --json
```

- **The stop** each way is where the joint's child link meets its parent link (each with the links
  fixed to it), whatever the other joints do. The finding also names the two parts that meet.
- **A clash**, said beside a stop, is anything the joint moves meeting another link first in this
  pose of the other joints: a self-collision of the pose, not the joint's range. Write the stop. A
  clash moves with the other joints (an arm drawn folded clashes its wrist on its shoulder a few
  degrees out; a thigh meets the torso only while the hip's other joints stand as drawn), and a
  simulator's contacts hold it, since the two links collide there. Where the hardware's own travel
  is narrower than the stop (a servo's position range), write that.
- **Units and zero.** Stops are in degrees or millimetres around the as-built pose, and in the
  joint's own values where its as-built value is not zero. Write them into the joint's
  `angular_range` or `linear_range` in the body, rounded towards zero, and run the model again.
  The command writes nothing.
- **What touches.** Two surfaces within `--clearance` (0.3 mm, the least it takes) count as
  touching, so a stop is where the parts all but touch: the joint's range. A larger clearance only
  narrows a range, stopping each joint where its parts first come that near (`--clearance 1`:
  within a millimetre). Every gap is measured to within 0.6 mm over the true one, never under it.
- **Touching or near as built.** Every pair is read against the as-built pose. Parts touching (a
  horn on its servo), or under 0.3 mm apart, meet only where their contact grows by about 15 mm^2
  on a surface that stops the motion, or where one is pushed into the other (a part resting face to
  face on its parent and turned into it stops where it lies), not where one slides along the other:
  a pin in its bore, a carriage on its rail or a link a little too wide for its clevis stops
  nothing. Parts a little farther apart (a jaw 0.5 mm from a servo's cover) meet only where their gap closes under half of what it was, less 0.3 mm (0.1 mm
  for a 0.5 mm gap), not where it narrows a hair. At a larger clearance the finding lists the
  pairs within it as built, `near as built:`, with the gap as built and at each stop, and a stop
  one of them makes says `closed to 0.2 from 0.5 mm as built`.
- **Turning on an output.** A vendor often draws a motor or a servo as one solid, its case and its
  output (flange, horn) together, and bolts the next link to that output: the link turns against a
  face of the solid it is bolted to. A pair touching as built on a surface about the joint's axis is
  read as an output and what turns on it: neither that face nor what of the solid lies within the
  reach of their contact about the axis (a locating boss, a pin, a bolt's seat through the face)
  stops the joint, and the finding lists the pair, `turns on: plate (link2) on motor (link1)`. The
  case beyond that reach, and every other part, still stops it. Where a stop a few degrees out still
  names that pair `touching as built`, the output carries something that reaches past its face (an
  arm, a cam) and that the hardware turns

```bash
curl -fsSL https://texttocad.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://www.texttocad.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. If the CAD app was
only just added, its server may still be starting: try again for up to a minute first. `cad doctor
--check` explains any other failure, changing nothing; `cad doctor` repairs what it reports. Tell the
person any next step `cad setup` prints.

One server runs for the installation: the first run starts it, every run and every
command goes through it, and it serves the viewer. `cad status` lists its workers
and the documents it holds; `cad stop` stops it.
A build cut off by the shell's time limit keeps running in the server; run the same
command again and it waits for that build and replays it (`cad status` shows it).
Give a cold build of a large model the shell tool's longest timeout, or run it in the
background.

Build every model with `cad run`, exactly like `uv run`: the same options and the same script
header, with nothing to set up. cad is pinned to this computer's release and its integrations come
from the script's imports (`import build123d` is the build123d integration), so a header names only
the script's own packages, never a version of cad:

```python
# /// script
# dependencies = ["pandas>=2"]
# ///
```

A one-off dependency is `--with`; a script inside a Python project runs with the project's
dependencies and lock. A run that stops on an import or a requirement says what to change in one
line. [Environments](references/environments.md) has the details: `--with`, projects and their locks,
private indexes and the network.

Command-line paths, and the paths `step.read`, `xbf.read`, `stl.read` and a type's `export`
take, are relative to the working directory, as are a model's own file reads. Anchor
them on `__file__` in code that must run from any folder.

## Write a model and run it

A part or an assembly is a function with no parameters, decorated `@model` (or with its
file decorators, never both), that returns a build123d shape. Its dimensions are the
arguments of a plain helper function, and each configuration is a `@model` of its own, with
its own id and page; constants several models share live in a module they import. A call
builds it and returns its document: a handle with `.id`, `.url`, `.shape` (the built shape)
and `.export(...)`. For example, `src/bracket.py`:

```python
import build123d as bd
from cad import model


def bracket_body(width, thickness, bore):
    body = bd.Box(width, 20, thickness)
    hole = bd.Cylinder(bore / 2, thickness)
    body = body - hole
    body.label = "bracket"
    body.color = "#4a6fa5"
    return body


@model
def bracket():
    return bracket_body(40, 6, 8)


@model
def bracket_wide():
    return bracket_body(60, 6, 8)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    bracket()
    bracket_wide()
```

```bash
cad run src/bracket.py
```

```text

  parts 1 · bounds 40 × 20 × 6 mm · joints 0 · sequences 0
  id: 0dc50a92-a21f-5895-a245-ebdeb5352f3b
  view: http://127.0.0.1:54360/0dc50a92-a21f-5895-a245-ebdeb5352f3b?token=...
built src/bracket.py::bracket_wide warm in 0.01s: bodies 1 run; 6 misses, 0 hits; body 0.01s, names 0.00s, document 0.00s
  parts 1 · bounds 60 × 20 × 6 mm · joints 0 · sequences 0
  id: 966d03a5-7b43-5bed-b75c-eb67d56c72d2
  view: http://127.0.0.1:54360/966d03a5-7b43-5bed-b75c-eb67d56c72d2?token=...
```

Each call the script's `__main__` makes prints how its model built, the delta under it
(parts, bounds, joints and sequences), its document's `id:` and its page, `view:` (the
handle's `.id` and `.url`). An unchanged rerun prints `took ... nothing ran` instead. Give the
user the page once ([Show the model](#show-the-model)) and use the id for every command
after it. The id comes from the
script's path and the function's name, or the script's folder and an explicit `@model(name="...")`,
so it is the same run after run, and the open page follows every run. A model's name is its identity
within its namespace, the function's name by default, `name=` gives it another. The namespace
is the script's folder; two explicit names in it must differ.

- **Running the script is the rebuild.** It writes no file. The server's warm worker for
  the script replays every operation an edit did not reach, so a comment re-runs nothing
  and a dimension edit re-runs what reads it
  ([what a run runs](references/model-contract.md#what-a-run-runs)). Decoration only
  declares: keep the calls under `if __name__ == "__main__":` so other scripts can import
  the models.
- **`@memo` marks stages, never parts.** The server already replays every kernel call, so
  mark only a function holding seconds of kernel work that an edit elsewhere leaves
  alone, such as a whole sub-assembly stage; never a part, never a helper called many
  times ([`@memo`](references/model-contract.md#memo-marks-stages)).
- **An assembly calls its parts.** Its body calls each part model and composes its shape
  (`plate().shape`), places and labels it, and returns a `Compound`. Each child builds in
  the same run and keeps its own document and id. Running a child's script alone leaves the assemblies that
  use it as they were: run the assembly.
- **`import build123d as bd`, and use it attribute-style** (`bd.Box`). The import is lazy:
  the kernel loads on first use, in the worker. `from build123d import Box`, or a
  module-level `bd.Color(...)` or `bd.Align` default, loads it at that line instead.
- **Colours are sRGB**, as a person picks them: `part.color = "#4a6fa5"` (`"#4a6fa5cc"` with
  alpha). `part.color` is build123d's: it takes no 0-255 integers (OCCT's `Color out`), which
  `paint` does. Import `metals` from `bd_materials`; assign a native material with
  `part.material = metals.aluminum()` (the families and their materials are listed in
  [colour and materials](references/build123d-modeling.md#colour-and-materials); plain steel is
  `metals.mild_steel()`); boards, electronic parts and finishes (solder mask, ENIG, anodized,
  powder coat) are `cad.build123d.materials`' named looks.
- **Inputs** are `step.read`, `xbf.read` and `stl.read` in the body, and any file its
  Python opens, each tracked by its bytes. The clock, environment variables and
  randomness are not seen: a body is a function of its code and its inputs. Compose
  project models by calling them, never by reading a file the project exported.
- **References** to faces, edges and parts come from `cad model inspect <id> [ref]`, and the
  body picks the same element with build123d's selectors; verify with a snapshot when in
  doubt ([references](references/inspection-and-validation.md#references)).
- **A shape with no function** (a notebook cell, a REPL) is handed over:
  `model(shape, name="plate")` returns the same handle, and no command builds it again.
- **The server never reruns code.** A restart reopens every document from the server's
  cache, as last built. When the cache holds no file of one (deleted by hand, or never
  saved), the page, `cad model inspect <id>` and `cad_show` print the command that brings it
  back (`cad run src/bracket.py`). Run it.
- Model units are millimetres, +Z up.
- An image without a scale sets no fit dimension, and a drawing's units, projection and
  revision decide how its numbers read. A missing or conflicting dimension that changes
  the result is the person's to settle; a value chosen in its place is an assumption.

## Files, when asked

A file is an action on the document the server holds, never part of the model: no code
change and no rebuild, written at once. It holds what the document held when it was
written, so a change made after it is in the file only once it is written again. Write one
when the person asks for it:

```bash
cad model export "$ID" STEP/bracket.step STL/bracket.stl GLB/bracket.glb 3MF/bracket.3mf
```

A project with standing deliverables gets an `exports.py` that imports its models and
calls `model.export(x, path, ...)` on each (`from cad import model`; `x` a model call's handle); running it rewrites every deliverable
([exports](references/exports.md)). An export takes a document and its destinations,
and nothing else: a posed file is a model that returns the posed assembly
(`posed(arm(), "folded")`), and a part on its own is the part's own model. A DXF is the export of a
model that returns 2D geometry, a profile or a flat pattern, and a solid is refused
([2D profiles and DXF](references/2d-profiles-and-dxf.md)). An STL or 3MF for printing a part with fits takes
`--tolerance MM`, about a tenth of its smallest clearance ([print tolerance](references/exports.md#print-tolerance)); a
GLB for another renderer takes `--tolerance MM --angle DEG` ([a GLB for another renderer](references/exports.md#a-glb-for-another-renderer)).
Those options mesh a GLB, an STL or a 3MF and nothing else, so an export that takes them names
only those files: a STEP, an xbf or a DXF among them refuses the whole export, nothing written.
Write the other files in an export of their own:

```bash
cad model export "$ID" STEP/bracket.step GLB/bracket.glb
cad model export "$ID" STL/bracket.stl 3MF/bracket.3mf --tolerance 0.02
```

The xbf, text-to-cad's own document, is Save As: export one only to share a model without its
code, or to compose it in another project with `xbf.read`. A restart needs none: the
server's own cache reopens every document it built, as last built. A vendor STEP is
converted to an xbf once
(`cad step export vendor/motor.step vendor/motor.xbf`) and read with `xbf.read`, many
times faster than parsing the STEP.

## Projects built around exported files

A project can instead revolve around its exported files, but only when the person asks to
iterate on the exported file itself or the project already does: an `exports.py`, a consumer
that reads the files (a robot description, a slicer, a drawing pipeline), or a 0.7-era
layout, whose runs wrote files. The loop is three steps. The script writes the file on each
run, by a file decorator in place of `@model` (`@step("../STEP/bracket.step")`, relative to
the script), or `exports.py` or `cad <type> export` follows the run. Show the file's page, not
the model's: it follows the file on disk, updating when a run rewrites the file.
Verification reads the file: `cad <type> snapshot` or `cad <type> inspect` with its path, or
`step.read` in a check. The costs keep the default the default: each iteration pays the
file's translation and the page's re-read, a STEP parsed again; a file names no model, so a
ref picked on its page has no `made_by` and a Quick Edit from it no way back into the code;
and the model's page stays the better place to look while editing.
[Exports](references/exports.md#model-page-or-file-page) tables the triggers and costs.

## Prompt references and inspection

A reference such as `0dc50a92-a21f-5895-a245-ebdeb5352f3b#bracket/face 7` names geometry
in a document by the server's own names: the document (a model's id, or a file's
absolute path), `#`, a part or an assembly by the labels on its way from the root
(`hand/finger.2` is the second component labelled `finger` in `hand`), then, after a
slash, one element by its name (`f:`, `e:`, `v:`) or its number (`face 7`). The CAD
viewer copies them. When a prompt names one, resolve it with `cad <type> inspect`:

```bash
cad model inspect "$ID" "bracket/face 7"
```

It answers in JSON what the ref names, placed where its occurrence stands: an element's
canonical `ref`, `kind`, `ordinal` and `name`, the kernel's facts (a face's `area`,
`centroid`, `surface`, `box`, `radius`; an edge's length and endpoints) and `made_by`,
the function, file and line of the code that made it; a part's or an assembly's volume
and mass. Edit the code `made_by` names, or pick the element in the body with
build123d's selectors (`body.faces().sort_by(bd.Axis.Z)[-1]`) matching those facts. A
ref resolves in the document as the latest run left it; one that names nothing, or
several things where it names one, is refused with what it could mean. The grammar is
in [references](references/inspection-and-validation.md#references).

A Quick Edit prompt names its document under `File:` (a model's id, or a file's path:
relative to your workspace, else from `~/`), selected entities under `References:`, and a
snapshot packet as inline JSON or a `.snapshot.json` path. Save inline JSON to a temporary `.snapshot.json`, and draw the view the person
drew their ink in, ink included:

```bash
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/quick_edit.png --annotation tmp/bracket.snapshot.json --camera authored
```

Inspect supplied annotations before editing. Without annotations, the captured view is
optional context; render it when useful to the request. After editing, run the script and
draw it again to check the change
([annotations and Quick Edit views](references/snapshot-review.md#annotations-and-quick-edit-views)).

A reference into a file that is not a document names what the viewer picked in it, in
that file's own terms (none is a ref `cad <type> inspect` resolves):

| File | Reference | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| URDF, SRDF | `/work/arm/arm.urdf#upper_arm` | the link `upper_arm` |
| GLB | `/work/out/model.glb#n12` | the glTF node `nodes[12]` (0-based, the file's own index) |
| 3MF | `/work/out/plate.3mf#o2.1` | the 2nd `<build><item>`'s 1st `<component>` (1-based); `#o3` is the 3rd build item |
| STL | the file alone, on `File:` | one mesh: nothing in it is picked |
| DXF | `/work/DXF/panel.dxf#h2F` | the modelspace entity whose handle is `2F`; what a block reference draws is named by its INSERT |

## Check each change

After every run, read its line and the delta under it (parts, bounds, joints, sequences): a
contradiction with what you intended is fixed before anything else. Then check the change the way it
can be checked:

| The change | Check it with |
| --- | --- |
| A number the person gave: a bound, a distance, a volume | An assert inside the model's body on what the geometry measures, or `cad model inspect`; never by restating the constant, never by code after the call in the script |
| A number the design implies: a clearance, a fit, a mass | A check script that calls the model ([below](#check-scripts)) |
| An assembly: parts added, moved or resized, a joint's travel | `cad model interference "$ID"`, with a `--pose` for each mechanism state and for each sequence at the times that matter ([below](#check-scripts)): no two parts share volume, exactly; a pair it could not measure is not a pass |
| New parts, placements, colours, a mechanism | The snapshots it takes to judge it: usually one from the angle that shows the change, more only when a view leaves the question open, a posed one for a mechanism state |
| A reference the prompt names | `cad model inspect "$ID" '<ref>'` ([Prompt references](#prompt-references-and-inspection)) |
| A 2D profile or DXF | `cad model export` (it runs the drawing checks), then an `ezdxf` read and `cad dxf snapshot` of the file ([check a drawing](references/2d-profiles-and-dxf.md#check-a-drawing)) |
| Any change to the geometry of a part whose process the request names or implies | Its process's check, with the same flags as before: the script's `Check:` line (`cad model dfm "$ID" ...`, [Design for the process](#design-for-the-process)); an error is fixed before anything else, a new warning fixed or reported |

```bash
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/review.png
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/top.png --camera top --display hidden-line
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/open.png --pose open
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/mid.png --pose cycle@2.5   # a configuration sequence, at a time of it
cad model snapshot "$ID" tmp/lit.png --preview          # lit in a studio: the picture for a person
```

A snapshot draws the document as the viewer does, rendered by OCCT, and writes nothing but the PNG.
Its options say how the picture is drawn: camera (`--camera top`), display, grid, pose and size
([snapshots](references/snapshot-review.md)). For a large assembly, isolate the parts the edit
touched or hide what covers them, instead of drawing the whole model.

- A number is never read off a picture: a snapshot shows arrangement and appearance, not dimensions.
- In an assembly, look at a part alone before it is placed, then the parts that move together, then a
  joint at both ends of its travel, and only then the whole, from behind as well as the front: a cover
  that half encloses what it covers is a few pixels of the whole model's picture and most of its own.
- A check that fails or cannot decide has shown nothing about the design.
- A retry that leaves out or shrinks a specified feature (a fillet skipped, a radius reduced) builds a
  different design from the one asked for.

### Joint stops

`cad <type> ranges` (`model`, `xbf`, `step`) finds each joint's stops from the parts themselves:
it turns or slides each joint alone from the as-built pose, the others as built, a degree or a
millimetre at a time each way, until the parts meet.

```bash
cad model ranges "$ID"
cad model ranges "$ID" --joint gripper
cad step ranges arm.step --step 0.5 --json
```

- **The stop** each way is where the joint's child link meets its parent link (each with the links
  fixed to it), whatever the other joints do. The finding also names the two parts that meet.
- **A clash**, said beside a stop, is anything the joint moves meeting another link first in this
  pose of the other joints: a self-collision of the pose, not the joint's range. Write the stop. A
  clash moves with the other joints (an arm drawn folded clashes its wrist on its shoulder a few
  degrees out; a thigh meets the torso only while the hip's other joints stand as drawn), and a
  simulator's contacts hold it, since the two links collide there. Where the hardware's own travel
  is narrower than the stop (a servo's position range), write that.
- **Units and zero.** Stops are in degrees or millimetres around the as-built pose, and in the
  joint's own values where its as-built value is not zero. Write them into the joint's
  `angular_range` or `linear_range` in the body, rounded towards zero, and run the model again.
  The command writes nothing.
- **What touches.** Two surfaces within `--clearance` (0.3 mm, the least it takes) count as
  touching, so a stop is where the parts all but touch: the joint's range. A larger clearance only
  narrows a range, stopping each joint where its parts first come that near (`--clearance 1`:
  within a millimetre). Every gap is measured to within 0.6 mm over the true one, never under it.
- **Touching or near as built.** Every pair is read against the as-built pose. Parts touching (a
  horn on its servo), or under 0.3 mm apart, meet only where their contact grows by about 15 mm^2
  on a surface that stops the motion, or where one is pushed into the other (a part resting face to
  face on its parent and turned into it stops where it lies), not where one slides along the other:
  a pin in its bore, a carriage on its rail or a link a little too wide for its clevis stops
  nothing. Parts a little farther apart (a jaw 0.5 mm from a servo's cover) meet only where their gap closes under half of what it was, less 0.3 mm (0.1 mm
  for a 0.5 mm gap), not where it narrows a hair. At a larger clearance the finding lists the
  pairs within it as built, `near as built:`, with the gap as built and at each stop, and a stop
  one of them makes says `closed to 0.2 from 0.5 mm as built`.
- **Turning on an output.** A vendor often draws a motor or a servo as one solid, its case and its
  output (flange, horn) together, and bolts the next link to that output: the link turns against a
  face of the solid it is bolted to. A pair touching as built on a surface about the joint's axis is
  read as an output and what turns on it: neither that face nor what of the solid lies within the
  reach of their contact about the axis (a locating boss, a pin, a bolt's seat through the face)

- **Overlapping as drawn.** A vendor's simplified parts are often drawn sunk into each other (a link

# Engineering drawing

An engineering drawing is a DOCUMENT derived from a part. `cad.eng_drawing`
projects views from the part's geometry, places dimensions between points ON
that geometry, finds centre marks on it, and lays the result out on an ISO
sheet with a frame and a title block. Change the model, rerun the drawing
script, and the views, hidden lines and measured values move with it. Nothing
on the sheet is drawn by hand, and nothing on it is a number you typed unless
you chose to override a value.

**The output is one PDF.** That is what a shop receives and what every
operating system opens. No DXF is written, nothing is paired or linked, and
there is no CLI: the script is the interface. Cut layouts and flat patterns are
toolpaths, not documents, and a different job.

## Setup

Run the `cad` command (`~/.local/bin/cad` where it is not on your PATH; `cad.exe` on Windows). If
it is missing, install text-to-cad, outside a sandbox or with its permission:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://texttocad.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://www.texttocad.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. If the CAD app was
only just added, its server may still be starting: try again for up to a minute first. `cad doctor
--check` explains any other failure, changing nothing; `cad doctor` repairs what it reports. Tell the
person any next step `cad setup` prints.

## Workflow

1. Get the part. Call the model: `enclosure()`, imported from the model's script,
   is built by text-to-cad's server (a replay when the server already holds it), and
   its `.shape` is the part. For a part with no model, read its file: `step.read` for a
   STEP, `xbf.read` for an xbf, anchored on `Path(__file__).parent`. Any build123d
   shape works. The drawing documents geometry, it does not build it.
2. Write `<name>_drawing.py` beside the model, from
   [the template](references/sheet-api.md#template). Import the model facts the
   dimensions reference (hole pitch, overall size, wall) from the model module
   rather than retyping them, so moving a feature moves its dimension.
3. Place views with `sheet.three_views(part, iso=True)`, which returns FOUR
   views: top, front and right in third angle with room for two rows of
   dimensions, plus an isometric in the free corner. `sheet.three_views(part)`
   returns three. Use `sheet.view(part, name, at=(x, y))` (sheet millimetres
   from the bottom-left corner; A3 is 420 × 297, A4 is 297 × 210) only for a
   custom layout.
4. Dimension what a maker needs, in MODEL coordinates: overall size per view
   (`view.overall()`), feature positions and sizes (`view.dim`, with `tol=`
   or `fit=` where the design requires one), holes as callouts (`view.hole`:
   thru, depth, counterbore, countersink, thread), and notes with leaders
   (`view.note`). Leave `text` unset so the dimension is measured; give a
   value only where the model does not define it. Leave `offset` unset too and
   the dimension takes the next free row outside the view; pass one only to
   place a dimension deliberately, and remember it is measured from the
   dimension's own points, not the view's edge. Keep notes few and short; one
   wider than the sheet's note column is refused, and `notes=` takes a LIST
   (`notes="BREAK EDGES"` is a sequence of eleven characters, so it is refused
   too).
5. Run `cad run <name>_drawing.py`. It prints the PDF it wrote, and **anything
   it noticed while drawing** — read those first:
   - *"measures blank paper"*: the dimension's model points do not land on the
     view's geometry. Almost always the part was built from a corner and the
     script assumed it was centred. Check the part's bounding box.
   - *"annotation overlaps"*: two callouts print on top of each other, usually
     one view's outermost dimension against the label of the view above it.
     Pass a bigger `three_views(gap=...)` or place one with `offset=`. The text
     is measured as the renderer draws it, glyph by glyph, so this fires on ink
     and not on markup: a chain of toleranced dimensions is silent when the
     values clear each other.

   Steps 3 and 5 stand on their own: a sheet of views with no dimensions on it
   yet is a drawing, and writes its PDF.

   When running unattended, set `MPLCONFIGDIR` to a writable directory so
   matplotlib's font cache does not warn.
6. **Read the PDF** and fix what collides. Check that no dimension text sits on
   a view, that hidden lines appear where features are behind faces, that every
   hole has a centre mark, and that no leader crosses the part. Very small
   dimensions (a few mm) put their value on their own extension line; dimension
   the larger feature instead. Move `at=` or `offset=` and rerun.

## What the sheet contains

- Layers with meaning: `VISIBLE` (heavy outline), `HIDDEN` (dashed), `CENTER`
  (centre marks), `DIM`, `NOTES`, `TITLE`, `SHEET` (frame), each printed at its
  own weight — 0.5 mm down to 0.18 mm, so thick reads against thin on paper.
  An edge is drawn once: a silhouette that the kernel returns as both visible
  and hidden stays on `VISIBLE`. Hidden TANGENT transitions are not drawn at
  all — a fillet running into a face, or the seam where a cylinder closes on
  itself, marks nothing a shop can see, and drawn dashed it reads as a hidden
  edge that is not there (on a bore, as a line down the hole's own axis).
- Dimensions measured from the geometry, with filled arrowheads and witness
  lines, and true-size values at any drawing scale.
- A title block with title, part number, material, author, scale, units,
  projection, revision, `SHEET n OF m` and the drawing function's name;
  numbered notes above it (the general tolerance, when given, is note 1);
  a revision table top-right when `revisions=` is given. Text longer than
  its cell is set smaller, and cut with an ellipsis rather than overrun.
- PDF bytes that are a function of the content: no creation date is stamped, so
  an unchanged drawing rebuilds to an identical file.

## What fails loudly

# Engineering drawing

An engineering drawing is a DOCUMENT derived from a part. `cad.eng_drawing`
projects views from the part's geometry, places dimensions between points ON
that geometry, finds centre marks on it, and lays the result out on an ISO
sheet with a frame and a title block. Change the model, rerun the drawing
script, and the views, hidden lines and measured values move with it. Nothing
on the sheet is drawn by hand, and nothing on it is a number you typed unless
you chose to override a value.

**The output is one PDF.** That is what a shop receives and what every
operating system opens. No DXF is written, nothing is paired or linked, and
there is no CLI: the script is the interface. Cut layouts and flat patterns are
toolpaths, not documents, and a different job.

## Setup

Run the `cad` command (`~/.local/bin/cad` where it is not on your PATH; `cad.exe` on Windows). If
it is missing, install text-to-cad, outside a sandbox or with its permission:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://texttocad.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://www.texttocad.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. If the CAD app was
only just added, its server may still be starting: try again for up to a minute first. `cad doctor
--check` explains any other failure, changing nothing; `cad doctor` repairs what it reports. Tell the
person any next step `cad setup` prints.

## Workflow

1. Get the part. Call the model: `enclosure()`, imported from the model's script,
   is built by text-to-cad's server (a replay when the server already holds it), and
   its `.shape` is the part. For a part with no model, read its file: `step.read` for a
   STEP, `xbf.read` for an xbf, anchored on `Path(__file__).parent`. Any build123d
   shape works. The drawing documents geometry, it does not build it.
2. Write `<name>_drawing.py` beside the model, from
   [the template](references/sheet-api.md#template). Import the model facts the
   dimensions reference (hole pitch, overall size, wall) from the model module
   rather than retyping them, so moving a feature moves its dimension.
3. Place views with `sheet.three_views(part, iso=True)`, which returns FOUR
   views: top, front and right in third angle with room for two rows of
   dimensions, plus an isometric in the free corner. `sheet.three_views(part)`
   returns three. Use `sheet.view(part, name, at=(x, y))` (sheet millimetres
   from the bottom-left corner; A3 is 420 × 297, A4 is 297 × 210) only for a
   custom layout.
4. Dimension what a maker needs, in MODEL coordinates: overall size per view
   (`view.overall()`), feature positions and sizes (`view.dim`, with `tol=`
   or `fit=` where the design requires one), holes as callouts (`view.hole`:
   thru, depth, counterbore, countersink, thread), and notes with leaders
   (`view.note`). Leave `text` unset so the dimension is measured; give a
   value only where the model does not define it. Leave `offset` unset too and
   the dimension takes the next free row outside the view; pass one only to
   place a dimension deliberately, and remember it is measured from the
   dimension's own points, not the view's edge. Keep notes few and short; one
   wider than the sheet's note column is refused, and `notes=` takes a LIST
   (`notes="BREAK EDGES"` is a sequence of eleven characters, so it is refused
   too).
5. Run `cad run <name>_drawing.py`. It prints the PDF it wrote, and **anything
   it noticed while drawing** — read those first:
   - *"measures blank paper"*: the dimension's model points do not land on the
     view's geometry. Almost always the part was built from a corner and the
     script assumed it was centred. Check the part's bounding box.
   - *"annotation overlaps"*: two callouts print on top of each other, usually
     one view's outermost dimension against the label of the view above it.
     Pass a bigger `three_views(gap=...)` or place one with `offset=`. The text
     is measured as the renderer draws it, glyph by glyph, so this fires on ink
     and not on markup: a chain of toleranced dimensions is silent when the
     values clear each other.

   Steps 3 and 5 stand on their own: a sheet of views with no dimensions on it
   yet is a drawing, and writes its PDF.

   When running unattended, set `MPLCONFIGDIR` to a writable directory so
   matplotlib's font cache does not warn.
6. **Read the PDF** and fix what collides. Check that no dimension text sits on
   a view, that hidden lines appear where features are behind faces, that every
   hole has a centre mark, and that no leader crosses the part. Very small
   dimensions (a few mm) put their value on their own extension line; dimension
   the larger feature instead. Move `at=` or `offset=` and rerun.

## What the sheet contains

- Layers with meaning: `VISIBLE` (heavy outline), `HIDDEN` (dashed), `CENTER`
  (centre marks), `DIM`, `NOTES`, `TITLE`, `SHEET` (frame), each printed at its
  own weight — 0.5 mm down to 0.18 mm, so thick reads against thin on paper.
  An edge is drawn once: a silhouette that the kernel returns as both visible
  and hidden stays on `VISIBLE`. Hidden TANGENT transitions are not drawn at
  all — a fillet running into a face, or the seam where a cylinder closes on
  itself, marks nothing a shop can see, and drawn dashed it reads as a hidden
  edge that is not there (on a bore, as a line down the hole's own axis).
- Dimensions measured from the geometry, with filled arrowheads and witness
  lines, and true-size values at any drawing scale.
- A title block with title, part number, material, author, scale, units,
  projection, revision, `SHEET n OF m` and the drawing function's name;
  numbered notes above it (the general tolerance, when given, is note 1);
  a revision table top-right when `revisions=` is given. Text longer than
  its cell is set smaller, and cut with an ellipsis rather than overrun.
- PDF bytes that are a function of the content: no creation date is stamped, so
  an unchanged drawing rebuilds to an identical file.

# FEA: will it hold, and how far does it move

A study holds some faces of a part, loads others, and has CalculiX solve the linear elastic
response on a netgen mesh of quadratic tetrahedra: stress and displacement under forces,
pressures, the part's own weight and a steady acceleration, with an isotropic material below
yield, perfectly rigid fixtures and loads that do not move. An assembly's parts are bonded where
they touch. It is a first-pass engineering check, not a certification; say so when you report.
Vibration, buckling, heat, flow, fatigue, impact and parts that slide on each other are not in
this version: say so plainly, and do not pass a static safety factor off as an answer to them. A
drop or a braking load can be estimated as a steady g-load
([Body loads](references/linear-static.md#body-loads-gravity-and-acceleration)).

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Check a part under a load** | `cad step solve part.step` lists its faces; write the study; solve into a folder. | [Workflow](#workflow), [Linear static](references/linear-static.md) |
| **Check an assembly** | `cad step solve assembly.step` lists the parts and the pairs that touch. | [Assemblies](#assemblies) |
| **Write or edit a study** | One JSON object: fixtures and loads, then material, mesh, margin and checks; parts and connections for an assembly. | [Study file](references/study-file.md) |
| **Choose a material** | The model's own (solve the model or its `.xbf`), or the E, ν and yield the user gives. | [Materials](references/materials.md) |
| **Judge the answer** | `result.json` and its findings, against a hand estimate. | [Findings](#findings), [Judging the answer](references/linear-static.md#judging-the-answer) |
| **Answer a question the summary does not** | `result.vtu`, read with meshio. | [Your own questions](#your-own-questions) |
| **Compare variants of a design** | The same study on each, faces mapped, mesh size held. | [Compare variants](#compare-variants) |

This skill studies a part; it does not model one. It reads a saved `.step` or `.xbf`, or a model the
engine holds by its document id (`cad model solve <id>`), and solves the whole document: to study one
part of an assembly alone, export it as a document of its own.

## Setup

Run the `cad` command (`~/.local/bin/cad` where it is not on your PATH; `cad.exe` on Windows). If
it is missing, install text-to-cad, outside a sandbox or with its permission:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://texttocad.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://www.texttocad.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. If the CAD app was
only just added, its server may still be starting: try again for up to a minute first. `cad doctor
--check` explains any other failure, changing nothing; `cad doctor` repairs what it reports. Tell the
person any next step `cad setup` prints.

The study is the `solve` operation of the document's type: `cad step solve`, `cad xbf solve`,
`cad model solve`. With no `--study` it lists the study's setup and writes nothing; with `--study`
and `--out DIR` it solves and writes its results into `DIR`. Its two tools are integrations the
`cad` command installs the first time a study needs them, nothing for you to install; `cad run`
gives a script that calls `cad.step.solve` both, with the kernel that reads the part.

- **netgen**, the mesher: the `netgen` integration (`cad[netgen]`, about 11 MB). netgen publishes
  it for macOS, Linux x86_64 and Windows x86_64 alone; elsewhere (Linux on ARM among them) a solve
  refuses, naming the platform.
- **CalculiX** (`ccx`), the solver: the `calculix` integration (`cad[calculix]`: the cad-ccx
  package, CalculiX 2.23 for each platform, about 13 MB). A person's own CalculiX is never run
  unless `CAD_CCX` names the file (2.20 or newer). It runs headless, on one thread, in a private
  folder, so the same study gives the same numbers every run, and every result names the version
  that solved it. `cad run ccx ARGS` runs that same `ccx` on a deck of your own.

Units are fixed: mm, N, MPa (pressure, modulus and stress), t/mm³ for density (steel 7.85e-9) and
g (9.81 m/s²) for gravity and acceleration. Restate every load in them before you write it down.

## Workflow

1. **List the faces.** A study names faces by the engine's refs, the ones the CAD Viewer copies; a
   face the user picked there arrives as `/work/bracket.step#bracket/face 17` and needs no lookup.

   ```bash
   cad step solve part.step
   ```

   With no study this is the setup, and writes nothing: the parts, the pairs that touch, then each
   face of the part, one a line: ref, area, centre, surface type and a hint such as `plane, normal
   -Z, largest`. Match the user's words ("the mounting face") to a ref by the hint and the centre;
   a hole is a `cylinder`. A document of several parts lists no faces until one is named:
   `cad step solve assembly.step --occurrence post`. A face number is a position in the saved
   document, so a part edited and written again is listed again before its study is re-run.

2. **Write the study** ([study-file.md](references/study-file.md)):

   ```json
   {
     "fixtures": [{"faces": ["bracket/face 17"], "type": "fixed"}],
     "loads": [{"faces": ["bracket/face 22"], "type": "force", "vector_N": [0, -500, 0]}]
   }
   ```

   `fixed` holds a face still; `roller` lets it slide in its plane but not off it (a frictionless
   support, or a symmetry cut). A `force` is the total over its faces; a `pressure` is in MPa,
   positive into the surface; `gravity` and `acceleration` take `vector_g` in g and no faces, and
   need the material's density. `margin` is the safety factor the part should keep (default 2, at
   least 1). `checks` adds a `displacement` check with the user's limit when they gave a sag or
   stiffness spec; left out, the stress check alone judges the part. Leave `mesh` out on the first
   run.

3. **Solve into a folder.**

   ```bash
   cad step solve part.step --study study.json --out /tmp/bracket-load --json
   ```

   `--out` is any folder, a temporary one included, made when missing; put it in the project when
   the user should keep the files. One folder per study: a solve replaces its own files there,
   touches nothing else, and a run that fails leaves the previous results as they were. It holds:

   | File | What it is for |
   | --- | --- |
   | `result.json` | the answer, what `--json` prints. Read this first. |
   | `stress.png`, `displacement.png` | the deformed part coloured by each field (blue low, red high), the deformation exaggerated by `deformation_scale`, with a colour bar giving the field, its units and its range. They show whether the load points the way you meant and which faces are held. Show the stress one to the user. |
   | `result.glb` | the same coloured surface, for any glTF viewer or `cad viewer` |
   | `result.vtu` | the volume mesh with `displacement` (mm) and `von_mises` (MPa) at its corner nodes ([Your own questions](#your-own-questions)) |
   | `ccx.inp` | with `--deck`: the input CalculiX solved (the finer solve's when there were two), for `cad run ccx -i ccx` in that folder |

   Where the engine cannot draw (Linux with no display) the pictures are left out and a
   `solver_note` says so; everything else is written.

   The result is a check's: `ok`, `findings` (each with `severity`, `code`, `message`, `location`
   and `hint`), `written`, and `measurements`: the study as given, the material, the faces it
   named (`named_faces`), the summary's figures (`max_von_mises_MPa` and `max_von_mises_at_mm`,
   `max_von_mises_gauss_MPa`, `yield_MPa`, `safety_factor`, `max_displacement_mm` and
   `max_displacement_at_mm`, `applied_force_N`, `reaction_force_N`, `deformation_scale`, `checks`;
   an assembly's `weakest_part` and `parts`), each fixture's reaction, `mesh` (size, elements,
   degrees of freedom, `straightened`, `solver`), `timings`, and `refined`, the first solve's size
   and peak when the run solved twice. Without `--json` the same prints as lines.

   - When the safety factor comes out under 3 the run meshes again finer (half the element size,
     less on a big model) and solves again by itself; the finer result is the one written
     ([Mesh](references/linear-static.md#mesh)).
   - Progress (`[fea] meshing ...`) goes to stderr, never into the result; `--verbose` adds mesh
     and solve detail there.
   - A malformed study (an unknown key, a face not on the part, a zero load, a load on a held
     face, no fixture) is refused before meshing, naming the field. A part the fixtures leave free
     to move, or that no load reaches, is refused by the solve; so is a solve whose reactions do
     not balance the applied load.
   - The command exits 1 (`"ok": false`) when a finding is an error: the part yields or misses a
     check, with the results written all the same; or the study stopped before the solve
     (`not_connected`), with nothing written. Warnings leave it at 0. Read the result either way.

4. **Report** with units: the peak von Mises and which feature it is near, the safety factor and
   the yield it is against (the low end of the model material's range), the max displacement and
   where, the applied load against the reaction, the mesh size and whether a finer re-solve ran;
   then the findings, what the model assumes, and what would change the answer most. Show
   `stress.png`, saying the deformation is exaggerated by `deformation_scale`.

## Your own questions

For anything the summary does not answer (the stress at the mounting holes, the sag along an
edge, how much of the part is above some stress), read `result.vtu` rather than solving again.
meshio or PyVista read it as it is (`uv run --with meshio`):

```python
import meshio, numpy as np

mesh = meshio.read("/tmp/bracket-load/result.vtu")
xyz, stress = mesh.points, mesh.point_data["von_mises"]          # mm, MPa
moved = np.linalg.norm(mesh.point_data["displacement"], axis=1)  # mm
near = np.linalg.norm(xyz - [42, 12, 3], axis=1) < 5             # within 5 mm of a point
print(stress[near].max(), moved[xyz[:, 2] > 49].max())
```

It holds the corner nodes of the tetrahedra, inside the part as well as on its skin; the reported
peak also counts the mid-edge nodes, so it can be a little higher than the VTU's own maximum. An
assembly's cells carry their part (`part`, the index into the summary's `parts`).

## Assemblies

A document of several parts is solved as one assembly: the parts that touch are bonded into one
conforming mesh, each keeps its own material, and each part's stress is judged against its own
yield. Every part must reach a fixed part through bonded neighbours. The keys are in
[study-file.md](references/study-file.md#assemblies).

The setup (`cad step solve assembly.step`) prints each part (ref, name, volume), then each pair:
`bonded`, with its contact area and gap; `not connected` for a near miss (a gap up to 1 mm, beyond
`contact_tolerance_mm`); `overlapping · N mm³` where the solids share volume, which is never
bonded. An overlap no deeper than the tolerance is an interference (a press fit, or a modelling
slip): it is listed `bonded` with `interference N mm` and closed like a gap. Read the listing
against the design: is each detected joint a real one, and is a joint you expect missing? It
judges by the 0.1 mm default; a study that should bond a wider gap sets `contact_tolerance_mm`
from the gap printed. Names can repeat (two parts called `bar`): use the ref (`frame/bar.2`) when
one does.

Each part is solved with its model's own material; `parts` gives a part the numbers the user
gives, and a part with no material in its model and none in the study is refused, naming it
([Materials](references/materials.md)). `connections` only overrides a detection (`free` for a
pair that must not be glued); touching pairs are bonded without it, and a pair set `free` inside a
group glued through other parts is refused. Fixtures and loads name faces on any part
(`post/face 23`), but not a face wholly covered by a bonded joint (refused, naming the face); a
face another part only partly covers is held or loaded on its uncovered area. Connections are
`bonded` or `free`: parts that press and slide on each other, and bolts, are not in this version.

The finer re-solve runs when the weakest part's safety factor is under 3. The summary's
`yield_MPa` and `safety_factor` are the weakest part's (`weakest_part`, `weakest_part_peak_MPa`),
while `max_von_mises_MPa` and `max_displacement_mm` span the whole assembly: the highest stress
can sit in a stronger part, so do not divide one by the other; each part's own numbers are in
`parts`. Each finding names its part ("'post' yields: ..."): fix that part (a thicker section, a
fillet, its material in `parts`, a larger joint, whose `area_mm2` is in the result's
`connections`), not the assembly in general.

## Compare variants

Each version of a design is its own document; run the same study on each into its own folder and
compare the `result.json`s. Face numbers are not stable between versions: an edit renumbers them,
and a ref reused unchecked lands on a different face with no error, so list each variant's faces
and map the baseline's by surface type, normal, centre and area, asking when two fit. Give every
study the baseline's `mesh.size_mm`, so a difference is the design's and not the mesh's, and give
the mapping (`baseline bracket/face 17 → bracket/face 21, the mounting face`) with the table so the
user can check it.

## Findings

Two von Mises peaks are reported. The **nodal** peak (`max_von_mises_MPa`, the one the safety factor
uses) is each element's stress at its integration points, extrapolated to its nodes and averaged
over the elements at a node, per part in an assembly; it is usually the higher of the two. The
**integration-point** peak (`max_von_mises_gauss_MPa`) is the raw element value; more than 50 %
above the nodal one, it means a concentration the mesh has not resolved. Safety factor = yield /
nodal peak of the solve that is written. The edge of a perfectly rigid fixture or bonded joint and
a sharp inside corner are singularities: the peak there grows with every refinement and never
converges, so the findings below say when to read the stress a little away from it instead.

Findings list errors first: an error makes the part unfit to use, a warning is a judgment to weigh
and act on or explain. Most carry the face (`bracket/face 12`, the original part's ref) when the
point is on one, and the point in mm. `peak_at_fixture` and `peak_concentration` appear only when
the safety factor is under the study's `margin` and a finer solve did not settle the peak (moved
it under 10 %); above the margin they would not change the answer.

| Finding | Severity | What it means | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `yields` | error | The nodal peak is above the material's yield. | Strengthen the part where the peak is, change the material, or confirm the load; a `peak_at_fixture` or `peak_concentration` beside it comes first: the peak may be the model's, not the part's. |
| `low_margin` | warning | It holds, but under the study's `margin`. | As for `yields`, or report the margin it has; never lower `margin` to clear the finding. |
| `displacement_over_limit` | error | A `displacement` check's largest displacement (over its faces, else the whole model) is past its `limit_mm`. | Stiffen the part, or confirm the limit with the user. |
| `peak_at_fixture` | warning | The peak sits on a fixed face or its edge, where a rigid clamp exaggerates stress, and a finer solve did not settle it. | Read the stress a little away from the face (the colours, or a probe in the VTU) before redesigning; if that is still high, the finding beside it stands. |
| `peak_concentration` | warning | The integration-point peak is well above the nodal one: a sharp corner or a concentrated load the mesh cannot resolve. | Under a safety factor of 3 the run already solved finer, so refining the whole part again is not the next step: fillet the corner or spread the load over a larger face. Above 3 (a high `margin`), refine once and compare ([Mesh](references/linear-static.md#mesh)). |
| `mesh_not_converged` | warning | The automatic finer solve moved the peak by more than 10 %. In an assembly, only for a part whose safety factor is under 3. | A peak that kept rising sits on a singularity: fillet it or judge the stress away from it. Otherwise set a smaller `mesh.size_mm` before trusting the safety factor. |
| `large_displacement` | warning | It moves more than 1 % of its size: the small-displacement model is stretched. | Check the fit against mating parts, and stiffen the part if the deflection is not acceptable. |
| `not_connected` | error | A part, or a group of parts, has no bonded chain to a fixed part; the solve did not run. The message names the nearest part and its distance. | Make the parts touch, fix a face on the group, or raise `contact_tolerance_mm` when the gap is one you would call touching. |
| `overlapping_parts` | warning | Two parts' solids overlap by more than the tolerance; they are not bonded. | Fix the geometry, or mark the pair `free` in `connections` when the overlap is an accepted shortcut (that silences it). A part held only through an overlap is `not_connected`. |
| `gap_closed` | warning | Two parts a little apart, or a little into each other, within the tolerance were bonded by moving geometry that far. | Check the gap is a modelling clearance and not a real one, or the interference a slip and not a press fit whose preload matters; the stress at that joint is the model's closing, not the part's. |
| `bonded_edge_peak` | warning | The peak sits on the edge of a bonded joint, where a rigid bond exaggerates stress; two meshes agreeing proves nothing there. | Read the stress a little away from the joint; a bolted or welded joint is softer than this model. |
| `solver_note` | warning | About the run itself: a slow solve past 150 000 degrees of freedom, a finer solve skipped or failed, pictures not drawn. | Mention it when it bears on the answer. |
