yield, perfectly rigid fixtures and loads that do not move. An assembly's parts are bonded where
they touch. It is a first-pass engineering check, not a certification; say so when you report.
Vibration, buckling, heat, flow, fatigue, impact and parts that slide on each other are not in
this version: say so plainly, and do not pass a static safety factor off as an answer to them. A
drop or a braking load can be estimated as a steady g-load
([Body loads](references/linear-static.md#body-loads-gravity-and-acceleration)).

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Check a part under a load** | `cad step solve part.step` lists its faces; write the study; solve into a folder. | [Workflow](#workflow), [Linear static](references/linear-static.md) |
| **Check an assembly** | `cad step solve assembly.step` lists the parts and the pairs that touch. | [Assemblies](#assemblies) |
| **Write or edit a study** | One JSON object: fixtures and loads, then material, mesh, margin and checks; parts and connections for an assembly. | [Study file](references/study-file.md) |
| **Choose a material** | The model's own (solve the model or its `.xbf`), or the E, ν and yield the user gives. | [Materials](references/materials.md) |
| **Judge the answer** | `result.json` and its findings, against a hand estimate. | [Findings](#findings), [Judging the answer](references/linear-static.md#judging-the-answer) |
| **Answer a question the summary does not** | `result.vtu`, read with meshio. | [Your own questions](#your-own-questions) |
| **Compare variants of a design** | The same study on each, faces mapped, mesh size held. | [Compare variants](#compare-variants) |

This skill studies a part; it does not model one. It reads a saved `.step` or `.xbf`, or a model the
engine holds by its document id (`cad model solve <id>`), and solves the whole document: to study one
part of an assembly alone, export it as a document of its own.

## Setup

Run the `cad` command (`~/.local/bin/cad` where it is not on your PATH; `cad.exe` on Windows). If
it is missing, install text-to-cad, outside a sandbox or with its permission:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://texttocad.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://www.texttocad.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. If the CAD app was
only just added, its server may still be starting: try again for up to a minute first. `cad doctor
--check` explains any other failure, changing nothing; `cad doctor` repairs what it reports. Tell the
person any next step `cad setup` prints.

The study is the `solve` operation of the document's type: `cad step solve`, `cad xbf solve`,
`cad model solve`. With no `--study` it lists the study's setup and writes nothing; with `--study`
and `--out DIR` it solves and writes its results into `DIR`. Its two tools are integrations the
`cad` command installs the first time a study needs them, nothing for you to install; `cad run`
gives a script that calls `cad.step.solve` both, with the kernel that reads the part.

- **netgen**, the mesher: the `netgen` integration (`cad[netgen]`, about 11 MB). netgen publishes
  it for macOS, Linux x86_64 and Windows x86_64 alone; elsewhere (Linux on ARM among them) a solve
  refuses, naming the platform.
- **CalculiX** (`ccx`), the solver: the `calculix` integration (`cad[calculix]`: the cad-ccx
  package, CalculiX 2.23 for each platform, about 13 MB). A person's own CalculiX is never run
  unless `CAD_CCX` names the file (2.20 or newer). It runs headless, on one thread, in a private
  folder, so the same study gives the same numbers every run, and every result names the version
  that solved it. `cad run ccx ARGS` runs that same `ccx` on a deck of your own.

Units are fixed: mm, N, MPa (pressure, modulus and stress), t/mm³ for density (steel 7.85e-9) and
g (9.81 m/s²) for gravity and acceleration. Restate every load in them before you write it down.

## Workflow

1. **List the faces.** A study names faces by the engine's refs, the ones the CAD Viewer copies; a
   face the user picked there arrives as `/work/bracket.step#bracket/face 17` and needs no lookup.

   ```bash
   cad step solve part.step
   ```

   With no study this is the setup, and writes nothing: the parts, the pairs that touch, then each
   face of the part, one a line: ref, area, centre, surface type and a hint such as `plane, normal
   -Z, largest`. Match the user's words ("the mounting face") to a ref by the hint and the centre;
   a hole is a `cylinder`. A document of several parts lists no faces until one is named:
   `cad step solve assembly.step --occurrence post`. A face number is a position in the saved
   document, so a part edited and written again is listed again before its study is re-run.

2. **Write the study** ([study-file.md](references/study-file.md)):

   ```json
   {
     "fixtures": [{"faces": ["bracket/face 17"], "type": "fixed"}],
     "loads": [{"faces": ["bracket/face 22"], "type": "force", "vector_N": [0, -500, 0]}]
   }
   ```

   `fixed` holds a face still; `roller` lets it slide in its plane but not off it (a frictionless
   support, or a symmetry cut). A `force` is the total over its faces; a `pressure` is in MPa,
   positive into the surface; `gravity` and `acceleration` take `vector_g` in g and no faces, and
   need the material's density. `margin` is the safety factor the part should keep (default 2, at
   least 1). `checks` adds a `displacement` check with the user's limit when they gave a sag or
   stiffness spec; left out, the stress check alone judges the part. Leave `mesh` out on the first
   run.

3. **Solve into a folder.**

   ```bash
   cad step solve part.step --study study.json --out /tmp/bracket-load --json
   ```

   `--out` is any folder, a temporary one included, made when missing; put it in the project when
   the user should keep the files. One folder per study: a solve replaces its own files there,
   touches nothing else, and a run that fails leaves the previous results as they were. It holds:

   | File | What it is for |
   | --- | --- |
   | `result.json` | the answer, what `--json` prints. Read this first. |
   | `stress.png`, `displacement.png` | the deformed part coloured by each field (blue low, red high), the deformation exaggerated by `deformation_scale`, with a colour bar giving the field, its units and its range. They show whether the load points the way you meant and which faces are held. Show the stress one to the user. |
   | `result.glb` | the same coloured surface, for any glTF viewer or `cad viewer` |
   | `result.vtu` | the volume mesh with `displacement` (mm) and `von_mises` (MPa) at its corner nodes ([Your own questions](#your-own-questions)) |
   | `ccx.inp` | with `--deck`: the input CalculiX solved (the finer solve's when there were two), for `cad run ccx -i ccx` in that folder |

   Where the engine cannot draw (Linux with no display) the pictures are left out and a
   `solver_note` says so; everything else is written.

   The result is a check's: `ok`, `findings` (each with `severity`, `code`, `message`, `location`
   and `hint`), `written`, and `measurements`: the study as given, the material, the faces it
   named (`named_faces`), the summary's figures (`max_von_mises_MPa` and `max_von_mises_at_mm`,
   `max_von_mises_gauss_MPa`, `yield_MPa`, `safety_factor`, `max_displacement_mm` and
   `max_displacement_at_mm`, `applied_force_N`, `reaction_force_N`, `deformation_scale`, `checks`;
   an assembly's `weakest_part` and `parts`), each fixture's reaction, `mesh` (size, elements,
   degrees of freedom, `straightened`, `solver`), `timings`, and `refined`, the first solve's size
   and peak when the run solved twice. Without `--json` the same prints as lines.

   - When the safety factor comes out under 3 the run meshes again finer (half the element size,
     less on a big model) and solves again by itself; the finer result is the one written
     ([Mesh](references/linear-static.md#mesh)).
   - Progress (`[fea] meshing ...`) goes to stderr, never into the result; `--verbose` adds mesh
     and solve detail there.
   - A malformed study (an unknown key, a face not on the part, a zero load, a load on a held
     face, no fixture) is refused before meshing, naming the field. A part the fixtures leave free
     to move, or that no load reaches, is refused by the solve; so is a solve whose reactions do
     not balance the applied load.
   - The command exits 1 (`"ok": false`) when a finding is an error: the part yields or misses a
     check, with the results written all the same; or the study stopped before the solve
     (`not_connected`), with nothing written. Warnings leave it at 0. Read the result either way.

4. **Report** with units: the peak von Mises and which feature it is near, the safety factor and
   the yield it is against (the low end of the model material's range), the max displacement and
   where, the applied load against the reaction, the mesh size and whether a finer re-solve ran;
   then the findings, what the model assumes, and what would change the answer most. Show
   `stress.png`, saying the deformation is exaggerated by `deformation_scale`.

## Your own questions

For anything the summary does not answer (the stress at the mounting holes, the sag along an
edge, how much of the part is above some stress), read `result.vtu` rather than solving again.
meshio or PyVista read it as it is (`uv run --with meshio`):

```python
import meshio, numpy as np

mesh = meshio.read("/tmp/bracket-load/result.vtu")
xyz, stress = mesh.points, mesh.point_data["von_mises"]          # mm, MPa
moved = np.linalg.norm(mesh.point_data["displacement"], axis=1)  # mm
near = np.linalg.norm(xyz - [42, 12, 3], axis=1) < 5             # within 5 mm of a point
print(stress[near].max(), moved[xyz[:, 2] > 49].max())
```

It holds the corner nodes of the tetrahedra, inside the part as well as on its skin; the reported
peak also counts the mid-edge nodes, so it can be a little higher than the VTU's own maximum. An
assembly's cells carry their part (`part`, the index into the summary's `parts`).

## Assemblies

A document of several parts is solved as one assembly: the parts that touch are bonded into one
conforming mesh, each keeps its own material, and each part's stress is judged against its own
yield. Every part must reach a fixed part through bonded neighbours. The keys are in
[study-file.md](references/study-file.md#assemblies).

The setup (`cad step solve assembly.step`) prints each part (ref, name, volume), then each pair:
`bonded`, with its contact area and gap; `not connected` for a near miss (a gap up to 1 mm, beyond
`contact_tolerance_mm`); `overlapping · N mm³` where the solids share volume, which is never
bonded. An overlap no deeper than the tolerance is an interference (a press fit, or a modelling
slip): it is listed `bonded` with `interference N mm` and closed like a gap. Read the listing
against the design: is each detected joint a real one, and is a joint you expect missing? It
judges by the 0.1 mm default; a study that should bond a wider gap sets `contact_tolerance_mm`
from the gap printed. Names can repeat (two parts called `bar`): use the ref (`frame/bar.2`) when
one does.

Each part is solved with its model's own material; `parts` gives a part the numbers the user
gives, and a part with no material in its model and none in the study is refused, naming it
([Materials](references/materials.md)). `connections` only overrides a detection (`free` for a
pair that must not be glued); touching pairs are bonded without it, and a pair set `free` inside a
group glued through other parts is refused. Fixtures and loads name faces on any part
(`post/face 23`), but not a face wholly covered by a bonded joint (refused, naming the face); a
face another part only partly covers is held or loaded on its uncovered area. Connections are
`bonded` or `free`: parts that press and slide on each other, and bolts, are not in this version.

The finer re-solve runs when the weakest part's safety factor is under 3. The summary's
`yield_MPa` and `safety_factor` are the weakest part's (`weakest_part`, `weakest_part_peak_MPa`),
while `max_von_mises_MPa` and `max_displacement_mm` span the whole assembly: the highest stress
can sit in a stronger part, so do not divide one by the other; each part's own numbers are in
`parts`. Each finding names its part ("'post' yields: ..."): fix that part (a thicker section, a
fillet, its material in `parts`, a larger joint, whose `area_mm2` is in the result's
`connections`), not the assembly in general.

## Compare variants

Each version of a design is its own document; run the same study on each into its own folder and
compare the `result.json`s. Face numbers are not stable between versions: an edit renumbers them,
and a ref reused unchecked lands on a different face with no error, so list each variant's faces
and map the baseline's by surface type, normal, centre and area, asking when two fit. Give every
study the baseline's `mesh.size_mm`, so a difference is the design's and not the mesh's, and give
the mapping (`baseline bracket/face 17 → bracket/face 21, the mounting face`) with the table so the
user can check it.

## Findings

Two von Mises peaks are reported. The **nodal** peak (`max_von_mises_MPa`, the one the safety factor
uses) is each element's stress at its integration points, extrapolated to its nodes and averaged
over the elements at a node, per part in an assembly; it is usually the higher of the two. The
**integration-point** peak (`max_von_mises_gauss_MPa`) is the raw element value; more than 50 %
above the nodal one, it means a concentration the mesh has not resolved. Safety factor = yield /
nodal peak of the solve that is written. The edge of a perfectly rigid fixture or bonded joint and
a sharp inside corner are singularities: the peak there grows with every refinement and never
converges, so the findings below say when to read the stress a little away from it instead.

Findings list errors first: an error makes the part unfit to use, a warning is a judgment to weigh
and act on or explain. Most carry the face (`bracket/face 12`, the original part's ref) when the
point is on one, and the point in mm. `peak_at_fixture` and `peak_concentration` appear only when
the safety factor is under the study's `margin` and a finer solve did not settle the peak (moved
it under 10 %); above the margin they would not change the answer.

| Finding | Severity | What it means | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `yields` | error | The nodal peak is above the material's yield. | Strengthen the part where the peak is, change the material, or confirm the load; a `peak_at_fixture` or `peak_concentration` beside it comes first: the peak may be the model's, not the part's. |
| `low_margin` | warning | It holds, but under the study's `margin`. | As for `yields`, or report the margin it has; never lower `margin` to clear the finding. |
| `displacement_over_limit` | error | A `displacement` check's largest displacement (over its faces, else the whole model) is past its `limit_mm`. | Stiffen the part, or confirm the limit with the user. |
| `peak_at_fixture` | warning | The peak sits on a fixed face or its edge, where a rigid clamp exaggerates stress, and a finer solve did not settle it. | Read the stress a little away from the face (the colours, or a probe in the VTU) before redesigning; if that is still high, the finding beside it stands. |
| `peak_concentration` | warning | The integration-point peak is well above the nodal one: a sharp corner or a concentrated load the mesh cannot resolve. | Under a safety factor of 3 the run already solved finer, so refining the whole part again is not the next step: fillet the corner or spread the load over a larger face. Above 3 (a high `margin`), refine once and compare ([Mesh](references/linear-static.md#mesh)). |
| `mesh_not_converged` | warning | The automatic finer solve moved the peak by more than 10 %. In an assembly, only for a part whose safety factor is under 3. | A peak that kept rising sits on a singularity: fillet it or judge the stress away from it. Otherwise set a smaller `mesh.size_mm` before trusting the safety factor. |
| `large_displacement` | warning | It moves more than 1 % of its size: the small-displacement model is stretched. | Check the fit against mating parts, and stiffen the part if the deflection is not acceptable. |
| `not_connected` | error | A part, or a group of parts, has no bonded chain to a fixed part; the solve did not run. The message names the nearest part and its distance. | Make the parts touch, fix a face on the group, or raise `contact_tolerance_mm` when the gap is one you would call touching. |
| `overlapping_parts` | warning | Two parts' solids overlap by more than the tolerance; they are not bonded. | Fix the geometry, or mark the pair `free` in `connections` when the overlap is an accepted shortcut (that silences it). A part held only through an overlap is `not_connected`. |
| `gap_closed` | warning | Two parts a little apart, or a little into each other, within the tolerance were bonded by moving geometry that far. | Check the gap is a modelling clearance and not a real one, or the interference a slip and not a press fit whose preload matters; the stress at that joint is the model's closing, not the part's. |
| `bonded_edge_peak` | warning | The peak sits on the edge of a bonded joint, where a rigid bond exaggerates stress; two meshes agreeing proves nothing there. | Read the stress a little away from the joint; a bolted or welded joint is softer than this model. |
| `solver_note` | warning | About the run itself: a slow solve past 150 000 degrees of freedom, a finer solve skipped or failed, pictures not drawn. | Mention it when it bears on the answer. |

# PCB design

## Setup

Run the `cad` command (`~/.local/bin/cad` where it is not on your PATH; `cad.exe` on Windows). If
it is missing, install text-to-cad, outside a sandbox or with its permission:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://texttocad.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://www.texttocad.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. If the CAD app was
only just added, its server may still be starting: try again for up to a minute first. `cad doctor
--check` explains any other failure, changing nothing; `cad doctor` repairs what it reports. Tell the
person any next step `cad setup` prints.

text-to-cad reads a board or schematic itself, so inspecting either, and viewing a schematic or taking
its snapshot, need no KiCad. DRC (`cad kicad_pcb drc`), ERC (`cad
kicad_sch erc`), every export (`cad kicad_pcb export`, `cad kicad_sch export`) and an edit
(`kicad_pcb.edit`, `kicad_sch.edit`) run KiCad's command line, `kicad-cli`,
and its IPC API from kicode, the `kicad` extra (`cad[kicad]`): the `cad` command installs it the first
time a board command needs it (about 100 MB to download and 340 MB on disk, once; nothing for you to install), and `cad run` gives a
script that edits a board its environment. Showing a board or taking its snapshot needs it too: KiCad
refills the board's copper pours on a copy before they are drawn, so the first board shown starts that
download. `CAD_KICAD_REFILL=0` in the server's environment turns the refill off (no download; set
it as `CAD_KICAD_3DMODELS` below), and the pours are drawn as the file saved them, as they are when the
download or the refill fails. A KiCad you installed yourself is never run. `CAD_KICAD_CLI` can name
another `kicad-cli` (the command line itself, named `kicad-cli`; KiCad 9 or newer, a nightly's for an
edit). It runs headless, with private settings, and never opens KiCad's app; never open a
board in KiCad's app to check it. Its library variables name KiCad's own libraries, never your
variables or KiCad settings: a project's `sym-lib-table` or `fp-lib-table` row that names a stock
library as KiCad's own tables do (`${KICAD10_SYMBOL_DIR}/Device.kicad_sym`,
`${KICAD10_FOOTPRINT_DIR}/Resistor_SMD.pretty`, any major's spelling) reads it in the libraries of the
KiCad you installed (the newest, if several; or the installation whose `3dmodels` folder
`CAD_KICAD_3DMODELS` names): nothing to set. With no KiCad installed, ERC warns `lib_symbol_issues` that
each such library was not found and DRC `lib_footprint_issues` that it is not enabled; a project that
carries its libraries (`${KIPRJMOD}`) needs no KiCad.

kicode's KiCad is a nightly (10.99), so a board or schematic it saves is in the nightly's format, which a
stable KiCad app refuses; viewing and snapshots still work, and the CAD Viewer's Open in says which KiCad on
this computer can open the file.

## Native files are the source

Edit the `.kicad_pcb` itself, preserving its companion `.kicad_pro`, `.kicad_dru`, libraries and
schematic when present. Reading or displaying a board never writes it. There is no text-to-cad PCB
model, build step, or generated-board ownership marker. A helper script may make a requested edit,
but reread the current file before editing and preserve unknown records and UUIDs. Do not regenerate
an existing project from an incomplete description.

Change a board through KiCad's IPC API in an edit, a `with` block: `kicad_pcb.edit` hands the block the
open board (KiPy's `Board`, as kicode names it: `kicode.board.Board`) and saves it at the block's end
when the block changed it; a block that changes nothing leaves the file byte for byte, one that raises
saves nothing (its exception goes on), and a save KiCad cannot finish leaves every file as it was,
saying why. A board not there yet is made by KiCad, with its project,
and saved. `kicad_sch.edit` does the same for a schematic ([schematic](references/schematic.md#edit-it));
the two of one project, one inside the other, share one KiCad. Run the script with `cad run board.py`,
which gives it the `kicad` extra (kicode: KiPy and a `kicad-cli` with its headless `api-server`); a
`kicad-cli` that `CAD_KICAD_CLI` names without one is refused up front, before any server starts. That
server listens on a local socket, which a shell sandbox that refuses sockets (an agent app's default, Codex's
among them) does not allow: the edit then stops at once, saying so, and the script must run outside the
sandbox (ask for the unsandboxed or escalated run); inspecting, DRC, exports and snapshots run inside it.
KiCad's first start from a new environment can take a minute, which the edit says while it waits. Import
KiPy's names from `kicode` (`from kicode.proto.common.types import KIID`, `from kicode.util.units import
from_mm`), never from `kipy`: the two cannot share a process. Saving writes the file in the nightly's
format: one from an older KiCad is upgraded, which the run says, and that older KiCad can no longer open
it. Checks and exports of the saved board are calls after the block (`kicad_pcb.drc`, `kicad_pcb.export`);
a STEP or GLB export holds each part's 3D model where the board's 3D view finds it ([board
views](#board-views)), and leaves out, naming them, the parts whose model is missing (or, in a STEP, only in
VRML); `--to dxf` writes the outline and drilled holes, for an enclosure:

```python
from cad import kicad_pcb
from kicode.util.units import from_mm

BOARD = "board.kicad_pcb"

with kicad_pcb.edit(BOARD) as b:       # the board file is the source; the block edits it in place
    power = [t for t in b.get_tracks() if t.net.name in {"+5V", "+3V3"}]
    for track in power:
        track.width = from_mm(0.8)
    b.update_items(power)
    b.refill_zones()
drc = kicad_pcb.drc(BOARD)
if not drc.ok:
    raise SystemExit("\n".join(drc.human_lines()))  # each finding, then FAILED and the count
for kind in ("gerbers", "drill", "pos", "bom", "step"):
    kicad_pcb.export(BOARD, to=kind, out=f"fab/{kind}")
```

An edit states the result it wants, so running it again is harmless: "U1 is at (10, 20)", "the power
tracks are 0.8 mm", never "move U1 5 mm" or "widen the tracks by 0.2 mm". Set absolute positions,
rotations, widths and nets; create an item only when the board does not hold it yet (find it first by its
reference, net or place). A script stopped halfway and run again then ends where one run would.

A board's design starts at its schematic, which says what connects to what: read it, check it with
ERC and look at each sheet ([schematic](references/schematic.md)) before laying out, and hold the board
to it after. For creation or structured edits read [native files](references/board-api.md). For parts and
footprints read [parts](references/parts.md). To place and route a board, read
[layout](references/layout.md): start from the schematic's netlist, place one part or functional
group at a time ([placement](references/placement.md) says in what order and where), route the nets
whose path matters by hand and direct the router (`cad.kicad.route` in the edit, with the plan you
give it; never a third-party autorouter) through the rest, octolinear, with widths for each net's
current, and check each step with `cad kicad_pcb drc`, the copper stills and a script of the layout's own properties. KiCad's file coordinates are millimetres, **y down**;
footprint-local positions and rotations must be transformed into the board frame. Use a net's
actual pad positions when routing. Check the datasheet's pin numbers, footprint orientation and
connector mating side; a plausible-looking layout does not establish electrical correctness.

## KiCad's own command line

Use the typed commands first (`cad kicad_pcb drc|export`, `cad kicad_sch erc|export`): their results are
the ones the checks and the viewer read. For anything they do not cover, run KiCad's own command line
with `cad run kicad-cli …`: the pinned kicode `kicad-cli` with its own subcommands and flags (`cad run
kicad-cli pcb --help`), no `--with` needed, headless with private settings, its output and exit code
KiCad's. `CAD_KICAD_CLI` does not change which one runs.

```bash
cad run kicad-cli pcb render --side top --rotate -45,0,45 -o tmp/board.png board.kicad_pcb
cad run kicad-cli project downgrade --dry-run --target 10.0 board.kicad_pro   # then -o DIR without --dry-run
```

Most commands write only their `-o`, though kicad-cli may leave a `.kicad_prl` beside a board it reads.
These rewrite the source: `pcb upgrade` and `sch upgrade`, `fp upgrade` and `sym upgrade` without `-o`,
and `pcb drc --refill-zones --save-board`. `project downgrade` exits 2 without writing when the target
cannot represent the board.

## Edit

1. Inspect the saved board with `from cad import kicad_pcb` in a script run with
   `cad run`; record the parts, nets, outline, relevant dimensions and constraints before
   changing it. [Checks](references/checks.md) documents this read-only API and clickable references.
2. Edit the board in a `kicad_pcb.edit` block (or, as a fallback, the native file). Keep net assignments,
   layer stack, track widths, clearances and custom rules consistent with the chosen fab and electrical

   adopt. If it cannot be checked, report the missing rule rather than invent one.

light one the same colours darkened enough to read (copper stays KiCad's red and blue).

are `board`, `copper`, `assembly`, and `placement`. A still is always light (the light canvas and its
colours), whatever the viewer's theme, as every snapshot is:

it is missing, install text-to-cad, outside a sandbox or with its permission:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://texttocad.dev/install.sh | sh
```

only just added, its server may still be starting: try again for up to a minute first. `cad doctor
--check` explains any other failure, changing nothing; `cad doctor` repairs what it reports. Tell the
person any next step `cad setup` prints.

its snapshot, need no KiCad. DRC (`cad kicad_pcb drc`), ERC (`cad
kicad_sch erc`), every export (`cad kicad_pcb export`, `cad kicad_sch export`) and an edit

time a board command needs it (about 100 MB to download and 340 MB on disk, once; nothing for you to install), and `cad run` gives a

refills the board's copper pours on a copy before they are drawn, so the first board shown starts that
download. `CAD_KICAD_REFILL=0` in the server's environment turns the refill off (no download; set
it as `CAD_KICAD_3DMODELS` below), and the pours are drawn as the file saved them, as they are when the
download or the refill fails. A KiCad you installed yourself is never run. `CAD_KICAD_CLI` can name

edit). It runs headless, with private settings, and never opens KiCad's app; never open a
board in KiCad's app to check it. Its library variables name KiCad's own libraries, never your
variables or KiCad settings: a project's `sym-lib-table` or `fp-lib-table` row that names a stock
library as KiCad's own tables do (`${KICAD10_SYMBOL_DIR}/Device.kicad_sym`,
`${KICAD10_FOOTPRINT_DIR}/Resistor_SMD.pretty`, any major's spelling) reads it in the libraries of the
KiCad you installed (the newest, if several; or the installation whose `3dmodels` folder
`CAD_KICAD_3DMODELS` names): nothing to set. With no KiCad installed, ERC warns `lib_symbol_issues` that
each such library was not found and DRC `lib_footprint_issues` that it is not enabled; a project that
carries its libraries (`${KIPRJMOD}`) needs no KiCad.

stable KiCad app refuses; viewing and snapshots still work, and the CAD Viewer's Open in says which KiCad on

and saved. `kicad_sch.edit` does the same for a schematic ([schematic](references/schematic.md#edit-it));

Show the person each model you create or change, and any model or file they ask to see. If your

graphic, as its Selection Filter ticks them (locked items only when the person ticks them), and a
drag draws a box that takes anything it touches. A box that takes nothing names an area, a box on the layer the person works on

hides and shows it, / searches it) has one search over three tabs. **Parts** lists the parts in the
schematic blocks their footprints record (by kind on a board that records none): a block picks every
part in it. **Nets** lists the nets: a net picks the whole net. Each arrives as a reference

bottom-right. Flip's and 2D/3D's icons are what is on screen and their tooltips what a press does. These are the display, so a Quick Edit's packet
draws the same. The board follows the app's theme: KiCad's colours on the dark canvas, and on the
light one the same colours darkened enough to read (copper stays KiCad's red and blue).

them, each part standing its 3D model. A press picks what the 2D view picks where the pointer's ray
meets the face, or the part whose body is in front of it; a drag turns the view; **Flip** (or ⇧F)
turns the camera over, and its icon shows the side the camera is on. A part's model is the STEP its footprint names, looked for only in the
board's folder (`${KIPRJMOD}`), KiCad's installed 3D library (every `${KICADn_3DMODEL_DIR}`) and the
folders `CAD_KICAD_3DMODELS` names (separated as `PATH` is); a `.wrl` name is read as the `.step` or
`.stp` beside it. `CAD_KICAD_3DMODELS` is read from the server's environment: a server already
running does not see a variable set in a shell afterwards, so set it before the server starts
(`cad stop`, then run any `cad` command with it set). A part without a model stands as a block, and

outside the folders above, too large, not a STEP, embedded in the board, or too many models.

missing with the reason, and the parts that name none), and a STEP or GLB export (`cad kicad_pcb export

the command's environment. `cad run kicad-cli` reads KiCad's library as KiCad does: every
`${KICADn_3DMODEL_DIR}` is the first of those library folders, and a `.wrl` name needs its `.wrl` file
there (KiCad 10's library ships STEP alone), so prefer the typed export.

are `board`, `copper`, `assembly`, and `placement`. A still is always light (the light canvas and its
colours), whatever the viewer's theme, as every snapshot is:

```bash
cad kicad_pcb snapshot board.kicad_pcb tmp/copper.png --display copper
cad kicad_pcb snapshot board.kicad_pcb tmp/bottom.png --display '{"mode":"copper","side":"bottom","poured":false}'
cad kicad_pcb snapshot board.kicad_pcb tmp/front.png --display '{"layers":["F.Cu","Edge.Cuts"]}'
cad kicad_pcb snapshot board.kicad_pcb tmp/inner.png --display '{"active":"In1.Cu","others":"dimmed","zones":0.3}'
cad kicad_pcb snapshot board.kicad_pcb tmp/front-only.png --display '{"active":"F.Cu","others":"hidden"}'
```

# 3D printing

Get a part printed: slice it for the person's printer and hand the print to the printer's app. The
part itself is designed with the cad skill, and whether it will print (walls, overhangs, supports,
orientation) is the cad skill's manufacturing check: run it first when the person asks. This skill
never starts a print.

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Slice it to G-code** | `python scripts/orca_presets.py --list machine --match "<printer>"` | [Slice with OrcaSlicer](#slice-with-orcaslicer) |
| **Print on a Bambu Lab printer** | The sliced `.gcode.3mf` | [Print on a Bambu Lab printer](#print-on-a-bambu-lab-printer) |
| **Will this print?** | The cad skill's printing check ($cad) | Its manufacturing references |

## Slice with OrcaSlicer

Slice with OrcaSlicer, headless (below) or by opening the model in the
OrcaSlicer app for the person. The agent never contacts a printer: for a Bambu
Lab printer, the result is sent through Bambu Connect ([below](#print-on-a-bambu-lab-printer));
for any other printer, give the person the `.gcode`.

### Install OrcaSlicer

- macOS: `brew install --cask orcaslicer`. The command line is
  `/Applications/OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer`.
- Windows and Linux: install a release from
  https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer/releases. The command is
  `orca-slicer`; on Linux, run it from the AppImage or Flatpak.

Below, `<orca>` is that command.

### Slice headless

OrcaSlicer's command line (https://www.orcaslicer.com/wiki/cli/cli_mode) needs
complete presets: it doesn't fill in a preset's parent settings, and it slices
only with a process whose compatible printers name the printer.
`scripts/orca_presets.py` (Python 3, no dependencies) writes them from
OrcaSlicer's presets, searching the person's own first, then OrcaSlicer's
built-in profiles.

1. Find the person's printer, process and filament presets. Prefer the presets
   they print with; never invent one, since a wrong bed size or
   temperature can damage the printer.

   ```bash
   python scripts/orca_presets.py --list machine --match "MK4S"
   python scripts/orca_presets.py --list process --match "@MK4S 0.4"
   python scripts/orca_presets.py --list filament --match "PLA @MK4S"
   ```

2. Write the complete presets:

   ```bash
   python scripts/orca_presets.py --printer "Prusa MK4S 0.4 nozzle" \
     --process "0.20mm SPEED @MK4S 0.4" --filament "Prusa Generic PLA @MK4S" \
     --out presets
   ```

3. Slice. Give `--outputdir` an absolute path:

   ```bash
   <orca> model.stl \
     --load-settings "presets/process.json;presets/printer.json" \
     --load-filaments presets/filament-1.json \
     --arrange 1 --slice 0 \
     --outputdir /absolute/path/to/out --export-3mf model.gcode.3mf
   ```

   This writes `plate_1.gcode`, the plain G-code, and `model.gcode.3mf`, the
   sliced 3MF, into that folder. The command line reads `.stl`,
   `.3mf`, `.obj` and `.amf`; export STEP to STL or 3MF first (for a text-to-cad model, `cad model export <id> part.3mf`, or `cad step export part.step part.3mf`).
   Override one setting with `--<setting>=<value>`, using the setting's key
   with hyphens for underscores, such as `--layer-height=0.16`.

### Open in OrcaSlicer

When the person would rather pick presets and slice themselves, or no preset can
be found, open the model in the app: `open -a OrcaSlicer model.stl` on macOS,
`Start-Process model.stl` on Windows when OrcaSlicer opens that file type, or
`orca-slicer model.stl` on Linux. The app also reads STEP.

## Print on a Bambu Lab printer

Bambu Lab printers take print jobs from other software only through Bambu
Connect, Bambu Lab's desktop app for third-party tools
(https://wiki.bambulab.com/en/software/third-party-integration). Open a sliced
file in Bambu Connect, or an unsliced model in Bambu Studio; the person
picks the printer and starts the print there. The agent never controls a
printer and never asks for access codes.

Bambu Connect runs on Windows 10 or later and macOS 13 or later, signed in to the
person's Bambu Lab account, with the printer on that account or reachable in LAN
mode (https://wiki.bambulab.com/en/software/bambu-connect). On Linux, where Bambu
Connect is still in development, use Bambu Studio.

| What the person has | Handoff |
| --- | --- |
| A sliced `.gcode.3mf`, from OrcaSlicer's command line or Bambu Studio's or OrcaSlicer's "Export plate sliced file" | Open it in Bambu Connect |
| A plain `.gcode` sliced with this printer's Bambu profile | Open it in Bambu Connect; if Bambu Connect refuses it, slice the model in Bambu Studio instead |
| A model with no slice: `.3mf`, `.stl` or `.step` (from a text-to-cad model: `cad model export <id> part.3mf`) | Open it in Bambu Studio, which slices it and sends it to the printer itself |

### Open a file in Bambu Connect

Bambu Connect imports a file from a `bambu-connect://import-file` link with
three parameters: `path`, the file's absolute path, and `name`, the name to
show, each percent-encoded the way JavaScript's `encodeURIComponent` does it
(Python: `urllib.parse.quote(value, safe="")`); and `version=1.0.0`. For
`/Users/me/prints/bracket.gcode.3mf`:

```text
bambu-connect://import-file?path=%2FUsers%2Fme%2Fprints%2Fbracket.gcode.3mf&name=bracket&version=1.0.0
```

Open the link with `open "<link>"` on macOS, or `Start-Process "<link>"` in
PowerShell on Windows. Bambu Connect comes forward with the file loaded.

### Open a model in Bambu Studio

On macOS run `open -a BambuStudio <file>` (some installs name the app
`Bambu Studio`). On Windows open the file from Bambu Studio's File menu, or run
`Start-Process <file>` when Bambu Studio is the file's default app. On Linux run
`bambu-studio <file>`, or open it from the AppImage or Flatpak.

### Finish in the app

Before the person presses Print, tell them what to check: the printer, plate
type, nozzle, filament and AMS mapping, a clear build plate, and someone nearby
for the first layer. Never report a print as started: the agent can't see the
printer, and the app shows the job and its progress.

Out of scope: starting, pausing or cancelling prints without the person, and
reading printer status. Bambu Lab's firmware takes those from other software
only through Bambu Connect, or in Developer Mode, which is LAN-only and
disconnects the printer from Bambu Cloud.

## Any other printer

The person prints the `.gcode` from their printer's app, its web interface
(PrusaLink, OctoPrint, Mainsail, Fluidd) or an SD card.

## Check each change

Before anyone prints a slice:

- `<orca> model.stl --info` prints the model's size; it has to fit the bed.
- Check the slice's settings, which OrcaSlicer writes at the end of the G-code:

  ```bash
  grep -E '^; (printer_model|nozzle_diameter|filament_type|nozzle_temperature|hot_plate_temp|bed_temperature) =|printing time' out/plate_1.gcode
  ```

  Confirm they match the person's printer and material before anyone prints it.

# Renders for people

A render is a picture for a person: a hero image, a README picture, a post, a turntable, a film of
a mechanism. The model goes to Blender as a GLB, loaded by `cad.blender.load`; the scene (camera,
lights, world, engine, output) is an ordinary Python script that imports `bpy`, Blender as a
Python module, and `cad run` runs it. Judge geometry with `cad model snapshot`, never with a
render: a render's lens, light and depth of field make it a poor measure, so never read a
dimension off one.

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |

# Robots and worlds for simulation and motion planning

A robot is described for its consumers in XML: a URDF for its structure (ROS, RViz,
robot_state_publisher), an SRDF beside it for MoveIt's planning semantics, and an MJCF for MuJoCo.
There are two routes to one:

- **Generate it from CAD.** A text-to-cad model that holds the mechanism (build123d joints, mechanism
  states, couplings), materials and the frames it names is written as an MJCF or a URDF by
  `cad model export`, or made a `mujoco.MjSpec` by `cad.mujoco.spec`, on which a MuJoCo function
  makes a simulation's choices (collision shapes, joint dynamics, actuators). Frames, limits, masses,
  inertias and meshes come from the kernel, exactly: the model is the source of truth, and the file
  is regenerated, never edited.
- **Author it by hand.** A robot with no CAD model here, an SRDF (always), a MuJoCo scene, or a file
  that already exists: the `.urdf`, `.srdf` or MJCF `.xml` is the source of truth, written
  and edited directly. The work is constrained kinematic modeling, not XML writing: the risks are
  frame placement, joint-axis semantics, units, mesh scale, inertial data and planning semantics, and
  a file can pass every check while placing a joint in the wrong spot.

## Setup

Run the `cad` command (`~/.local/bin/cad` where it is not on your PATH; `cad.exe` on Windows). If
it is missing, install text-to-cad, outside a sandbox or with its permission:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://texttocad.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://www.texttocad.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. If the CAD app was
only just added, its server may still be starting: try again for up to a minute first. `cad doctor
--check` explains any other failure, changing nothing; `cad doctor` repairs what it reports. Tell the
person any next step `cad setup` prints.

`cad doctor --check` also reports the installation in use and the server's release. A URDF's and an
SRDF's validation need nothing beyond the Python standard library; a snapshot and a generated description draw on the CAD
kernel. `cad mujoco check` and `cad run mujoco-studio` use MuJoCo's headless core
and Studio's web viewer, `cad[mujoco]` (about 20 MB), which the `cad` command fetches into an
environment of its own the first time and reuses after; a script run by `cad run` that imports
`mujoco` gets the same. `decompose()` in a MuJoCo function uses CoACD, `cad[coacd]` (one wheel,
about 3 MB), which the engine likewise fetches into an environment of its own the first time a part
is decomposed, and reuses after. `cad <verb> --help` gives the complete current interface.

## Generate from CAD

The CAD model declares what the geometry determines, and the writers turn it into each format.
Everything below is written in the model's body (the `cad` skill's kinematics reference has the
mechanism):

- **The mechanism** is the links and joints: build123d's `RevoluteJoint`, `LinearJoint`,
  `CylindricalJoint` and `BallJoint` connected with `connect_to`. The as-built pose is every joint's
  zero in the description, and each joint's limits are its range around that zero. Where the robot
  has a controller, the description's zero is the controller's zero, so that a joint value means the
  same in the simulator and on the hardware; where none exists yet, build the mechanism at the pose a
  simulator should start from (fingers open, arm straight). A vendor's STEP is often drawn at its
  controller's zero: its published ranges fit the swept stops around the pose drawn (the vendor-STEP
  recipe's step 6 says how to tell). Where the controller's zero is another pose, name that pose a
  mechanism state and export with `--zero <state>`: every body stands as the state poses it, each
  joint counts from there (its limits and the other states shifted with it), and the CAD stays as
  drawn. Where the hardware's stops are the parts meeting, find them from the parts:
  `cad model ranges <id>` turns or slides each joint alone until its child link meets its parent and
  prints each stop, in degrees or millimetres around the as-built pose; write them into the joint's
  `angular_range` or `linear_range`, rounded towards zero, and run the model again (the `cad` skill's
  Joint stops section has the options). A servo's own travel, narrower than that, is the datasheet's.
  A joint `ranges` finds clear all the way round (a wrist roll) has no stop in the parts. Give it
  the actuator's own travel from its datasheet (a position servo's one turn, `angular_range=(-180,
  180)` around the pose its encoder centres on), which is a limited hinge in MJCF and a `revolute`
  in URDF. Where the hardware turns without end (a slip ring, a wheel), use `angular_range=(-math.inf,
  math.inf)`: a hinge with no range in MJCF, a `continuous` joint in URDF.
- **The base link.** Name the link the robot stands on `base_link` (`link(base, "base_link")`), the
  frame ROS tools expect. Where that link has a mass or stands off the world's origin, the URDF
  roots at an empty `base_footprint` on a fixed joint above it, as REP 105 roots a base, because
  KDL takes no inertia on the root; `base_link` keeps its name and stays the robot's base frame. A
  root of another name gets an empty `base_link` above it instead.
- **Mechanism states** (`mechanism_state(assembly, "home", ...)`) are the named poses, MJCF keys
  (a URDF holds no poses). Name one `home`, the pose a person and a controller start from: the zero
  itself where the hardware starts there, another state where it does not.
- **Couplings** (`gear_pair`, `rack_and_pinion_pair`) are a follower joint on its leader: MJCF's
  `<equality><joint>`, URDF's `<mimic>`. Two slides a pinion drives (a parallel gripper) couple
  through a `RevoluteJoint` on the palm connected to nothing, named first in the
  `rack_and_pinion_pair`, where the CAD draws no pinion: the file has no body or joint for it, and
  the second slide follows the first, one control as on the hardware.
- **Closed loops** (a four-bar, a slider-crank): connect the joints of a tree from the ground,
  then pair the loop's last joint by label where both parts already stand. The MJCF closes the
  loop there with an equality between a site on each body (a hinge two `connect`s, a ball one;
  where the last joint is a slide, at the loop's nearest hinge or ball instead); the URDF leaves
  that joint out and says so. A loop's joints have no named pose and no stops from `cad model
  ranges`.
- **Materials** (`bd_materials`, `part.material = metals.aluminum()`) give each part a density, so
  each link's mass, centre of mass and inertia tensor are the kernel's, exact. A part with no material
  weighs nothing, and a link of such parts has no inertial ([Inertials](references/inertials.md)).
- **`mass(part_or_assembly, grams)`** is what the hardware weighs (a scale's reading, a datasheet's):
  the solids below it keep their densities' ratios (one density for all where none of them has a material; a part with no material among parts that have one carries none of the total, and the export says so) and are
  scaled alike to make up `grams`, so the centre of mass and the inertia's shape stay the geometry's.
  An inner `mass()` fixes its own subtree; an outer one scales only the solids no inner one holds.
- **`point_mass(part, grams, at, name=, inertia=)`** is a lump the CAD leaves out (a motor inside a
  filled housing), at `at` in the part's own frame, no inertia of its own unless `inertia=(ixx, iyy,
  izz)` (kg*m^2) gives it. A `mass()` above it counts it: the lumps are fixed and the solids make up
  the rest, and a total the lumps reach or pass is refused.
- **`frame(part, name, location)`** names a frame on a part (a tool point, a camera mount, a sensor),
  in the part's own frame, the one its geometry is in before it is placed; it is a site in MJCF.
- **`body(part, name=None)`** keeps a part a body of its own, fixed to the link it would merge into (a
  camera mount, a fingertip the simulator addresses), with its own mass and geoms.
- **`limits(assembly, joint, effort=, velocity=)`**: a joint's drive limits from its datasheet, N*m
  or N and rad/s or m/s, the URDF's `<limit>` and MJCF's `actuatorfrcrange` (MJCF has no speed
  bound). Without them a URDF says `effort="0" velocity="0"`, which a ROS controller reads literally;
  a joint given only one of the two has the other written 0, and the export's log names it. Joint
  dynamics, actuators and contact are a simulation's choices, made in its
  [MuJoCo function](#the-mujoco-function).
- **`free(assembly)`** says the robot is not bolted to the world (a humanoid, a quadruped, a mobile
  base, a part dropped on a table): on the top assembly, its base floats, an MJCF `<freejoint>` (its
  seven values in every key, the base where it stands) and a URDF's root, which floats already. The
  floating base's frame stands at its link's centre of mass, its axes the model's: a humanoid's at its
  torso, not on the floor between its feet, so a key's first three values and the simulator's base
  position read where the base is (a URDF fixes it to an empty root at the model's origin, `base_link`,
  or `base_footprint` where the base is named `base_link`). Mount an IMU or a camera on a `frame()` of
  the torso's part, not on the base frame. Bolted is the default, an arm on a bench. On a part or a sub-assembly of a model with no joints, that
  node's body alone floats.
- **`link(part_or_assembly, name)`** names the link its parts make (`base_link`, `upper_arm_link`)
  where the first part's label is not the name a consumer wants. A link otherwise takes its jointed
  assembly's label (the `Compound` that holds its joint), else its first part's; a body is named by
  `body()`. Two links of one name, or one link's parts declaring two, are refused by name.

```python
from cad.build123d import body, frame, free, limits, link, mass, point_mass

frame(palm, "tcp", bd.Pos(0, 0, 65))   # mm, in the palm's own frame
body(camera, "camera")                 # fixed to the palm, a body of its own
limits(root, "left", effort=2, velocity=1.5)   # N*m, rad/s: the servo's datasheet
point_mass(palm, 120, bd.Pos(0, 0, 20), name="motor")   # g, mm in the palm's own frame
mass(palm, 410)                        # g: the palm as weighed, its motor included
link(palm, "base_link")                # the palm's link, named as ROS names a base
free(root)                             # on a mobile base: not bolted to the world
```

Then run the model, find its stops where they are the parts' (`cad model ranges`), and write the
file from the document the run left in the server (`$ID` is the `id:` line the run printed); the
suffix picks the format, and the meshes are written as binary STL
in metres beside it:

```bash
cad run src/gripper.py
cad model ranges "$ID"
cad model export "$ID" sim/gripper.xml
cad model export "$ID" description/gripper.urdf --zero home
cad step export vendor/part.step sim/part.xml
```

Each robot export says what it wrote after the file's line: its links and how its base stands, its
joints by kind, its total mass, then its couplings, loops, frames, collisions, the contact excludes
the file holds (the jointed pairs touching at rest), keys and zero; every warning (a link with no
mass, a joint left out) is a line of the export's log before it. `--json` gives the same as the file
row's `robot`. Read it before anything else: a mass of 0, a link you did not expect or a missing
joint is a model to fix.

An MJCF export to `sim/gripper.xml` writes `sim/scene.xml` beside it when there is none:
a scene that includes the robot's file and adds a floor, a light and a skybox, so `cad run
mujoco-studio --model sim/scene.xml` opens it standing on something. The scene is yours to edit
(solver settings, cameras, other bodies); an export never writes over it and says it kept it.

A plain export is laid out as published MuJoCo robots are (radians, `meshdir="assets"`,
`autolimits`, `implicitfast`, a `visual` class in group 2 that collides with nothing and a
`collision` class in group 3, explicit `<inertial>`s, a site per frame, a key per state); what each
format drops is in [Interoperability](references/interoperability.md#one-description-two-writers).
**It holds no chosen collision shape, no joint dynamics and no actuator**: each part collides as its
own mesh (MuJoCo collides a mesh as its convex hull), and nothing drives or holds its joints. Those
are a simulation's choices, made in a [MuJoCo function](#the-mujoco-function). A floor, lights,
solver settings and other robots are the scene's. A plain export needs no MuJoCo. A STEP has no
mechanism: each of its top-level parts is a body hung fixed from the world. A robot's STEP is
articulated in a model first ([from a vendor STEP](references/from-a-vendor-step.md)).

- **Never edit a generated file.** A change to a frame, a limit, a mass or a mesh is a change to the
  model: edit it, run it, export again. A collision shape, a damping or an actuator is a change to
  the MuJoCo function: edit it and run it again. A floor, solver settings and an arm from elsewhere go in
  the scene.
- **Check what the kernel cannot know**: that each joint's positive motion is the one intended, and
  that the collision shapes suit the physics. A generated file can still have its joint signs wrong
  if the model does.

### The MuJoCo function

The model carries what is true of the machine. What a simulation chooses (each part's collision
shape, contact friction, excluded pairs, joint armature, damping and dry friction, actuators,
sensors) goes in a MuJoCo function: a plain Python function, in a script beside the model, that
makes the robot a `mujoco.MjSpec` with `spec()`, makes those choices on it in MuJoCo's own API and
returns it. The script's `__main__` saves it:

```python
# src/gripper_mujoco.py
import mujoco
from cad.mujoco import collisions, fit, save, spec

from gripper import gripper


def gripper_mujoco() -> mujoco.MjSpec:
    s = spec(gripper())
    for part in ("palm", "left", "right"):
        fit(s, part, "box")                        # the kernel's box of the part's exact solid
    for geom in collisions(s, "left") + collisions(s, "right"):
        geom.friction = [1.1, 0.005, 0.0001]       # sliding, torsional, rolling
    left = s.joint("left")
    left.armature = 0.002                          # kg*m^2
    left.damping = [0.1, 0, 0]                     # N*m*s/rad, a 3-vector in MuJoCo 4.0.0
    grip = s.add_actuator(name="grip", target="left", trntype=mujoco.mjtTrn.mjTRN_JOINT)
    grip.set_to_position(kp=20, dampratio=1, inheritrange=True)
    return s


if __name__ == "__main__":
    save(gripper_mujoco(), "sim/gripper.xml")
```

```bash
cad run src/gripper_mujoco.py
cad mujoco check sim/scene.xml
```

`fit`, `decompose`, `collisions` and `parts` are the only helpers: the first three name a part by its
label path, as `cad model inspect` prints it, and `parts(s)` lists every path. Everything else (`armature`, `damping`, `frictionloss`,
`add_exclude`, `add_actuator`, sensors, keys) is MuJoCo's API, used directly. `save` writes the file
with its meshes in `assets/` beside it, so the folder travels, and a `scene.xml` beside it when there
is none, then prints the check's warnings, what the model collides as (`collisions:`) and its
contact excludes (`excludes:`): read both lines against the choices the function made. This file
replaces the plain export: a robot's own file carries its actuators. The helpers, what `save` does, and MuJoCo 4.0.0's traps are in
[MuJoCo environment](references/mujoco-environment.md#the-mujoco-function), with a scene composed
around it.

## How the formats fit together

- **URDF** owns physical robot structure: links, joints, geometry, inertials, limits, mimic
  joints, transmissions, and robot-state publishing.
- **SRDF** owns MoveIt semantics on top of a valid URDF: virtual joints, passive joints, planning
  groups, group states, end effectors, and disabled collision pairs. It pairs with its URDF by
  colocation and robot name alone: same folder, same `<robot name>`, exactly one such URDF.
- **MJCF** owns a MuJoCo model: bodies, joints, geoms, default classes, actuators, equalities and
  keyframes, in one file or a `scene.xml` that includes the robot's.
- **Meshes** are owned by the CAD workflow: a generated description writes them itself, and a
  hand-authored one takes one asset per link, exported in that link's frame, its source units
  recorded. Fix a wrong export there, never with URDF origins or MJCF body positions.

Names are identifiers every consumer shares: SRDF groups, controllers and TF read the URDF's link
and joint names, so a rename updates every consumer in the same task, and any URDF edit re-runs
`cad srdf validate` on the SRDF beside it ([Interoperability](references/interoperability.md)).

## Rules for every format

1. Identify the target consumers first: RViz, robot_state_publisher, MoveIt, a real robot driver,
   MuJoCo or another simulator, and how strict they are.
2. Before writing XML by hand, establish the ledger (frames, joints, geometry, units, assumptions)
   and keep it as a comment block at the top of the file. Update it in the same edit that changes
   the modeled facts; a stale ledger is worse than none. A number the kernel computed is not
   ledgered: it is regenerated. A generated file has no ledger; the model is its source.
3. SI units: meters, kilograms, seconds, radians, unless the target explicitly requires otherwise.
   URDF limits and SRDF group states never hold degrees; an MJCF says `<compiler angle="radian"/>`,
   since MuJoCo's default is degrees. These are the files' units: a snapshot's `--pose` takes
   degrees (metres for a slide), as `cad model snapshot` does
   ([Check each change](#check-each-change)).
4. Do not infer spatial transforms, mesh units, handedness, axes, joint signs or planning
   semantics from vague prose or visual impression. Use CAD transforms, dimensioned drawings,
   measured values, existing source data, simulator documentation, or explicit documented
   assumptions ([Guardrails](references/guardrails.md)).
5. Never freehand computed numbers (inertia tensors, centers of mass, unit conversions across many
   links, mirrored transforms, adjacency lists). Where a CAD model exists, generate them from it;
   otherwise compute them with closed-form formulas or a throwaway helper script. A helper is
   scaffolding; for complex or parametric models it may be kept on disk beside related model source
   and named in the ledger, and the checked-in XML stays canonical: regenerating is an explicit
   editing action, never an implicit build step.
6. Never encode a kinematic fix by offsetting only a visual mesh; correct the link and joint
   frames, unless the mesh is genuinely offset from its link frame.
7. Regenerate upstream geometry, mesh and robot-description assets with their owning workflows
   before editing a description that references them.
8. Check every created or modified file ([below](#check-each-change)) and report the checks run,
   the checks skipped, the assumptions and the risks
   ([report shape](references/guardrails.md#the-report)).

### URDF

The robot's tree of links and joints. Most URDF errors are frame errors: a joint's `<origin>` is
the parent-link-frame transform to the joint frame at zero position, the child link frame
coincides with the joint frame, `<axis>` is expressed in the joint frame, and the
skills.bodyMd:
# Robots and worlds for simulation and motion planning

A robot is described for its consumers in XML: a URDF for its structure (ROS, RViz,
robot_state_publisher), an SRDF beside it for MoveIt's planning semantics, and an MJCF for MuJoCo.
There are two routes to one:

- **Generate it from CAD.** A text-to-cad model that holds the mechanism (build123d joints, mechanism

  makes a simulation's choices (collision shapes, joint dynamics, actuators). Frames, limits, masses,
  inertias and meshes come from the kernel, exactly: the model is the source of truth, and the file
  is regenerated, never edited.
- **Author it by hand.** A robot with no CAD model here, an SRDF (always), a MuJoCo scene, or a file
  that already exists: the `.urdf`, `.srdf` or MJCF `.xml` is the source of truth, written
  and edited directly. The work is constrained kinematic modeling, not XML writing: the risks are
  frame placement, joint-axis semantics, units, mesh scale, inertial data and planning semantics, and
  a file can pass every check while placing a joint in the wrong spot.

| **Open an existing URDF, SRDF or MJCF** | Show it to the person: a URDF or an SRDF in the CAD Viewer, an MJCF in MuJoCo Studio. | [Show the model](#show-the-model) |

## Setup

Run the `cad` command (`~/.local/bin/cad` where it is not on your PATH; `cad.exe` on Windows). If
it is missing, install text-to-cad, outside a sandbox or with its permission:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://texttocad.dev/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://www.texttocad.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. If the CAD app was
only just added, its server may still be starting: try again for up to a minute first. `cad doctor
--check` explains any other failure, changing nothing; `cad doctor` repairs what it reports. Tell the
person any next step `cad setup` prints.

`cad doctor --check` also reports the installation in use and the server's release. A URDF's and an
SRDF's validation need nothing beyond the Python standard library; a snapshot and a generated description draw on the CAD
kernel. `cad mujoco check` and `cad run mujoco-studio` use MuJoCo's headless core
and Studio's web viewer, `cad[mujoco]` (about 20 MB), which the `cad` command fetches into an
environment of its own the first time and reuses after; a script run by `cad run` that imports
`mujoco` gets the same. `decompose()` in a MuJoCo function uses CoACD, `cad[coacd]` (one wheel,
about 3 MB), which the engine likewise fetches into an environment of its own the first time a part
is decomposed, and reuses after. `cad <verb> --help` gives the complete current interface.

## Generate from CAD

The CAD model declares what the geometry determines, and the writers turn it into each format.
Everything below is written in the model's body (the `cad` skill's kinematics reference has the
mechanism):

- **The mechanism** is the links and joints: build123d's `RevoluteJoint`, `LinearJoint`,
  `CylindricalJoint` and `BallJoint` connected with `connect_to`. The as-built pose is every joint's
  zero in the description, and each joint's limits are its range around that zero. Where the robot
  has a controller, the description's zero is the controller's zero, so that a joint value means the
  same in the simulator and on the hardware; where none exists yet, build the mechanism at the pose a
  simulator should start from (fingers open, arm straight). A vendor's STEP is often drawn at its
  controller's zero: its published ranges fit the swept stops around the pose drawn (the vendor-STEP
  recipe's step 6 says how to tell). Where the controller's zero is another pose, name that pose a
  mechanism state and export with `--zero <state>`: every body stands as the state poses it, each
  joint counts from there (its limits and the other states shifted with it), and the CAD stays as
  drawn. Where the hardware's stops are the parts meeting, find them from the parts:
  `cad model ranges <id>` turns or slides each joint alone until its child link meets its parent and
  prints each stop, in degrees or millimetres around the as-built pose; write them into the joint's
  `angular_range` or `linear_range`, rounded towards zero, and run the model again (the `cad` skill's
  Joint stops section has the options). A servo's own travel, narrower than that, is the datasheet's.
  A joint `ranges` finds clear all the way round (a wrist roll) has no stop in the parts. Give it
  the actuator's own travel from its datasheet (a position servo's one turn, `angular_range=(-180,
  180)` around the pose its encoder centres on), which is a limited hinge in MJCF and a `revolute`
  in URDF. Where the hardware turns without end (a slip ring, a wheel), use `angular_range=(-math.inf,
  math.inf)`: a hinge with no range in MJCF, a `continuous` joint in URDF.
- **The base link.** Name the link the robot stands on `base_link` (`link(base, "base_link")`), the
  frame ROS tools expect. Where that link has a mass or stands off the world's origin, the URDF
  roots at an empty `base_footprint` on a fixed joint above it, as REP 105 roots a base, because
  KDL takes no inertia on the root; `base_link` keeps its name and stays the robot's base frame. A
  root of another name gets an empty `base_link` above it instead.
- **Mechanism states** (`mechanism_state(assembly, "home", ...)`) are the named poses, MJCF keys
  (a URDF holds no poses). Name one `home`, the pose a person and a controller start from: the zero
  itself where the hardware starts there, another state where it does not.
- **Couplings** (`gear_pair`, `rack_and_pinion_pair`) are a follower joint on its leader: MJCF's
  `<equality><joint>`, URDF's `<mimic>`. Two slides a pinion drives (a parallel gripper) couple
  through a `RevoluteJoint` on the palm connected to nothing, named first in the
  `rack_and_pinion_pair`, where the CAD draws no pinion: the file has no body or joint for it, and
  the second slide follows the first, one control as on the hardware.
- **Closed loops** (a four-bar, a slider-crank): connect the joints of a tree from the ground,
  then pair the loop's last joint by label where both parts already stand. The MJCF closes the
  loop there with an equality between a site on each body (a hinge two `connect`s, a ball one;
  where the last joint is a slide, at the loop's nearest hinge or ball instead); the URDF leaves
  that joint out and says so. A loop's joints have no named pose and no stops from `cad model
  ranges`.
- **Materials** (`bd_materials`, `part.material = metals.aluminum()`) give each part a density, so
  each link's mass, centre of mass and inertia tensor are the kernel's, exact. A part with no material
  weighs nothing, and a link of such parts has no inertial ([Inertials](references/inertials.md)).
- **`mass(part_or_assembly, grams)`** is what the hardware weighs (a scale's reading, a datasheet's):
  the solids below it keep their densities' ratios (one density for all where none of them has a material; a part with no material among parts that have one carries none of the total, and the export says so) and are
  scaled alike to make up `grams`, so the centre of mass and the inertia's shape stay the geometry's.
  An inner `mass()` fixes its own subtree; an outer one scales only the solids no inner one holds.
- **`point_mass(part, grams, at, name=, inertia=)`** is a lump the CAD leaves out (a motor inside a
  filled housing), at `at` in the part's own frame, no inertia of its own unless `inertia=(ixx, iyy,
  izz)` (kg*m^2) gives it. A `mass()` above it counts it: the lumps are fixed and the solids make up
  the rest, and a total the lumps reach or pass is refused.
- **`frame(part, name, location)`** names a frame on a part (a tool point, a camera mount, a sensor),
  in the part's own frame, the one its geometry is in before it is placed; it is a site in MJCF.
- **`body(part, name=None)`** keeps a part a body of its own, fixed to the link it would merge into (a
  camera mount, a fingertip the simulator addresses), with its own mass and geoms.
- **`limits(assembly, joint, effort=, velocity=)`**: a joint's drive limits from its datasheet, N*m
  or N and rad/s or m/s, the URDF's `<limit>` and MJCF's `actuatorfrcrange` (MJCF has no speed
  bound). Without them a URDF says `effort="0" velocity="0"`, which a ROS controller reads literally;
  a joint given only one of the two has the other written 0, and the export's log names it. Joint
  dynamics, actuators and contact are a simulation's choices, made in its
  [MuJoCo function](#the-mujoco-function).
- **`free(assembly)`** says the robot is not bolted to the world (a humanoid, a quadruped, a mobile
  base, a part dropped on a table): on the top assembly, its base floats, an MJCF `<freejoint>` (its
  seven values in every key, the base where it stands) and a URDF's root, which floats already. The
  floating base's frame stands at its link's centre of mass, its axes the model's: a humanoid's at its
  torso, not on the floor between its feet, so a key's first three values and the simulator's base
  position read where the base is (a URDF fixes it to an empty root at the model's origin, `base_link`,
  or `base_footprint` where the base is named `base_link`). Mount an IMU or a camera on a `frame()` of
  the torso's part, not on the base frame. Bolted is the default, an arm on a bench. On a part or a sub-assembly of a model with no joints, that
  node's body alone floats.
- **`link(part_or_assembly, name)`** names the link its parts make (`base_link`, `upper_arm_link`)
  where the first part's label is not the name a consumer wants. A link otherwise takes its jointed
  assembly's label (the `Compound` that holds its joint), else its first part's; a body is named by
  `body()`. Two links of one name, or one link's parts declaring two, are refused by name.

```python
from cad.build123d import body, frame, free, limits, link, mass, point_mass

frame(palm, "tcp", bd.Pos(0, 0, 65))   # mm, in the palm's own frame
body(camera, "camera")                 # fixed to the palm, a body of its own
limits(root, "left", effort=2, velocity=1.5)   # N*m, rad/s: the servo's datasheet
point_mass(palm, 120, bd.Pos(0, 0, 20), name="motor")   # g, mm in the palm's own frame
mass(palm, 410)                        # g: the palm as weighed, its motor included
link(palm, "base_link")                # the palm's link, named as ROS names a base
free(root)                             # on a mobile base: not bolted to the world
```

Then run the model, find its stops where they are the parts' (`cad model ranges`), and write the
file from the document the run left in the server (`$ID` is the `id:` line the run printed); the
suffix picks the format, and the meshes are written as binary STL
in metres beside it:

```bash
cad run src/gripper.py
cad model ranges "$ID"
cad model export "$ID" sim/gripper.xml
cad model export "$ID" description/gripper.urdf --zero home
cad step export vendor/part.step sim/part.xml
```

Each robot export says what it wrote after the file's line: its links and how its base stands, its
joints by kind, its total mass, then its couplings, loops, frames, collisions, the contact excludes
the file holds (the jointed pairs touching at rest), keys and zero; every warning (a link with no
mass, a joint left out) is a line of the export's log before it. `--json` gives the same as the file
row's `robot`. Read it before anything else: a mass of 0, a link you did not expect or a missing
joint is a model to fix.

An MJCF export to `sim/gripper.xml` writes `sim/scene.xml` beside it when there is none:
a scene that includes the robot's file and adds a floor, a light and a skybox, so `cad run
mujoco-studio --model sim/scene.xml` opens it standing on something. The scene is yours to edit
(solver settings, cameras, other bodies); an export never writes over it and says it kept it.

A plain export is laid out as published MuJoCo robots are (radians, `meshdir="assets"`,
`autolimits`, `implicitfast`, a `visual` class in group 2 that collides with nothing and a
`collision` class in group 3, explicit `<inertial>`s, a site per frame, a key per state); what each
format drops is in [Interoperability](references/interoperability.md#one-description-two-writers).
**It holds no chosen collision shape, no joint dynamics and no actuator**: each part collides as its
own mesh (MuJoCo collides a mesh as its convex hull), and nothing drives or holds its joints. Those
are a simulation's choices, made in a [MuJoCo function](#the-mujoco-function). A floor, lights,
solver settings and other robots are the scene's. A plain export needs no MuJoCo. A STEP has no
mechanism: each of its top-level parts is a body hung fixed from the world. A robot's STEP is
articulated in a model first ([from a vendor STEP](references/from-a-vendor-step.md)).

- **Never edit a generated file.** A change to a frame, a limit, a mass or a mesh is a change to the
  model: edit it, run it, export again. A collision shape, a damping or an actuator is a change to
  the MuJoCo function: edit it and run it again. A floor, solver settings and an arm from elsewhere go in
  the scene.
- **Check what the kernel cannot know**: that each joint's positive motion is the one intended, and
  that the collision shapes suit the physics. A generated file can still have its joint signs wrong
  if the model does.

### The MuJoCo function

The model carries what is true of the machine. What a simulation chooses (each part's collision
shape, contact friction, excluded pairs, joint armature, damping and dry friction, actuators,
sensors) goes in a MuJoCo function: a plain Python function, in a script beside the model, that
makes the robot a `mujoco.MjSpec` with `spec()`, makes those choices on it in MuJoCo's own API and
returns it. The script's `__main__` saves it:

```python
# src/gripper_mujoco.py
import mujoco
from cad.mujoco import collisions, fit, save, spec

from gripper import gripper


def gripper_mujoco() -> mujoco.MjSpec:
    s = spec(gripper())
    for part in ("palm", "left", "right"):
        fit(s, part, "box")                        # the kernel's box of the part's exact solid
    for geom in collisions(s, "left") + collisions(s, "right"):
        geom.friction = [1.1, 0.005, 0.0001]       # sliding, torsional, rolling
    left = s.joint("left")
    left.armature = 0.002                          # kg*m^2
    left.damping = [0.1, 0, 0]                     # N*m*s/rad, a 3-vector in MuJoCo 4.0.0
    grip = s.add_actuator(name="grip", target="left", trntype=mujoco.mjtTrn.mjTRN_JOINT)
    grip.set_to_position(kp=20, dampratio=1, inheritrange=True)
    return s


if __name__ == "__main__":
    save(gripper_mujoco(), "sim/gripper.xml")
```

```bash
cad run src/gripper_mujoco.py
cad mujoco check sim/scene.xml
```

`fit`, `decompose`, `collisions` and `parts` are the only helpers: the first three name a part by its
label path, as `cad model inspect` prints it, and `parts(s)` lists every path. Everything else (`armature`, `damping`, `frictionloss`,
`add_exclude`, `add_actuator`, sensors, keys) is MuJoCo's API, used directly. `save` writes the file
with its meshes in `assets/` beside it, so the folder travels, and a `scene.xml` beside it when there
is none, then prints the check's warnings, what the model collides as (`collisions:`) and its
contact excludes (`excludes:`): read both lines against the choices the function made. This file
replaces the plain export: a robot's own file carries its actuators. The helpers, what `save` does, and MuJoCo 4.0.0's traps are in
[MuJoCo environment](references/mujoco-environment.md#the-mujoco-function), with a scene composed
around it.

## How the formats fit together

- **URDF** owns physical robot structure: links, joints, geometry, inertials, limits, mimic
  joints, transmissions, and robot-state publishing.
- **SRDF** owns MoveIt semantics on top of a valid URDF: virtual joints, passive joints, planning
  groups, group states, end effectors, and disabled collision pairs. It pairs with its URDF by
  colocation and robot name alone: same folder, same `<robot name>`, exactly one such URDF.
- **MJCF** owns a MuJoCo model: bodies, joints, geoms, default classes, actuators, equalities and
  keyframes, in one file or a `scene.xml` that includes the robot's.
- **Meshes** are owned by the CAD workflow: a generated description writes them itself, and a
  hand-authored one takes one asset per link, exported in that link's frame, its source units
  recorded. Fix a wrong export there, never with URDF origins or MJCF body positions.

Names are identifiers every consumer shares: SRDF groups, controllers and TF read the URDF's link
and joint names, so a rename updates every consumer in the same task, and any URDF edit re-runs
`cad srdf validate` on the SRDF beside it ([Interoperability](references/interoperability.md)).

## Rules for every format

1. Identify the target consumers first: RViz, robot_state_publisher, MoveIt, a real robot driver,
   MuJoCo or another simulator, and how strict they are.
2. Before writing XML by hand, establish the ledger (frames, joints, geometry, units, assumptions)
   and keep it as a comment block at the top of the file. Update it in the same edit that changes
   the modeled facts; a stale ledger is worse than none. A number the kernel computed is not
   ledgered: it is regenerated. A generated file has no ledger; the model is its source.
3. SI units: meters, kilograms, seconds, radians, unless the target explicitly requires otherwise.
   URDF limits and SRDF group states never hold degrees; an MJCF says `<compiler angle="radian"/>`,
   since MuJoCo's default is degrees. These are the files' units: a snapshot's `--pose` takes
   degrees (metres for a slide), as `cad model snapshot` does
   ([Check each change](#check-each-change)).
4. Do not infer spatial transforms, mesh units, handedness, axes, joint signs or planning
   semantics from vague prose or visual impression. Use CAD transforms, dimensioned drawings,
   measured values, existing source data, simulator documentation, or explicit documented
   assumptions ([Guardrails](references/guardrails.md)).
5. Never freehand computed numbers (inertia tensors, centers of mass, unit conversions across many
   links, mirrored transforms, adjacency lists). Where a CAD model exists, generate them from it;
   otherwise compute them with closed-form formulas or a throwaway helper script. A helper is
   scaffolding; for complex or parametric models it may be kept on disk beside related model source
   and named in the ledger, and the checked-in XML stays canonical: regenerating is an explicit
   editing action, never an implicit build step.
6. Never encode a kinematic fix by offsetting only a visual mesh; correct the link and joint
   frames, unless the mesh is genuinely offset from its link frame.
7. Regenerate upstream geometry, mesh and robot-description assets with their owning workflows
   before editing a description that references them.
8. Check every created or modified file ([below](#check-each-change)) and report the checks run,
   the checks skipped, the assumptions and the risks
   ([report shape](references/guardrails.md#the-report)).

## Author by hand

Each section below is a format written directly. For a robot that has a CAD model here, generate the
URDF or MJCF instead ([above](#generate-from-cad)) and author only what it does not carry: the
SRDF, a MuJoCo scene.

### URDF

The robot's tree of links and joints. Most URDF errors are frame errors: a joint's `<origin>` is
the parent-link-frame transform to the joint frame at zero position, the child link frame
coincides with the joint frame, `<axis>` is expressed in the joint frame, and the `visual`,
`collision` and `inertial` origins are each expressed in the link frame, independently
([Frames](references/urdf-frames.md)).

1. Identify the `.urdf` and its consumers; read or create the ledger

2. Prepare mesh assets first when links reference meshes ([Meshes](references/meshes.md)).
3. Author the XML per the [authoring contract](references/urdf-authoring.md): links in tree order,
